Aargau is a German-speaking canton of mixed urban-rural character in the northern midlands, with its main centres at Aarau, Baden and Wettingen and a wider hinterland of smaller communities. It leans more politically and socially conservative than the national average, and LGBT infrastructure is far less visible outside the towns: visitors read as trans may notice staring, misgendering or unsolicited curiosity in places with less everyday exposure to gender diversity. Everyday friction rather than official hostility is the realistic expectation here.

No Aargau-specific restriction on trans visitors' access to facilities or healthcare, no documented police or border campaign targeting gender-nonconforming people, and no known local pattern of anti-trans violence or official harassment distinguishes the canton from the national picture. Aargau's cantonal detention law carries no documented gender-identity provision — an absence of a local protective layer rather than a documented exposure — so custody treatment would rest on cantonal practice and individual circumstances, and this remains the main open question for a trans visitor. The canton has also not adopted a conversion-therapy ban of its own. Policing, courts and health services in Aargau are professional and accessible, so a trans person outed here is more likely to face bureaucratic inconsistency and social friction than state hostility.

regions.name: Basel-Landschaft
regions.merged_summary:
Basel-Landschaft is subject to Switzerland's national regime in full, with no local exception. It is a prosperous, German-speaking half-canton wrapping around the city of Basel — a mix of commuter suburbs, small towns and rural Jura foothills rather than a city in its own right — with no canton-specific restriction, facility ban or entry rule targeting trans visitors documented, and no recorded pattern of hostile official practice. Basel's hospitals, universities and region-wide support services, including Transgender Network Switzerland and Dialogai, are a short distance away.

Local conditions shape day-to-day exposure more than law. The canton is more rural and moderately conservative than neighbouring Basel-Stadt, so staring, awkward misgendering or uneven service responses are more plausible away from the Basel fringe, and nightlife and community visibility are thinner than in the city canton. One concrete local gap: Basel-Stadt's detention law explicitly requires that a detained person's gender identity be respected, and no equivalent cantonal custody rule is documented for Basel-Landschaft, so placement in custody there remains a matter of discretionary practice. The likely consequence of discovery is social friction rather than state action, though local complaint handling and facility responses are not well documented.

regions.name: Luzern
regions.merged_summary: Luzern is subject to Swiss national law in full, with no cantonal exception of its own. The canton is Catholic and socially traditional, and its LGBTIQ-specific support infrastructure is thinner than in Zurich, Geneva or Basel, so a visitor needing local services may have to rely on the national helplines and networks. The city of Lucerne itself is a major international tourist destination with a cosmopolitan, visitor-facing centre, while the surrounding countryside is more rural and politically conservative, meaning social friction is likelier outside the city than within it. Everyday friction is more likely to take the form of staring, misgendering or awkward service interactions than of official hostility, and no local policy targeting trans visitors, or pattern of official targeting, is documented. Foreign identity documents are ordinarily accepted in ordinary settings. Cantonal detention rules here carry no explicit gender-identity placement clause, so any custody exposure would rest on general practice rather than a written local guarantee. The lack of a documented local incident is not evidence that none occurs: knowledge of everyday treatment is uneven, and uncertainty about individual encounters remains.

regions.name: Neuchâtel
regions.merged_summary: Neuchâtel is subject to Switzerland's national regime in full, with no cantonal exception. A French-speaking lakeside canton in western Switzerland, it is urban and centred on Neuchâtel city and La Chaux-de-Fonds, with a lakeside tourism economy and a progressive voting profile. It was the first Swiss canton to bring a ban on conversion therapy into force, in 2023 — a local institutional signal of how the canton views such practices, though not itself a safeguard for a visitor. Everyday tourist settings are routine: no canton-specific campaign targeting trans visitors, hostile legislation, harsh border screening or documented local pattern of police hostility is known here, and policing and civil institutions are generally rights-respecting. Residual friction is ordinary rather than structural — staring, misgendering, bureaucratic confusion — and is likelier outside the main towns. Custody is the genuinely uncertain exposure: placement of detainees is cantonal, and Neuchâtel has no gender-identity provision in its detention law of the kind Basel-Stadt adopted in 2019, so practice in an emergency would be discretionary rather than codified. No documented local hostility distinguishes the canton, but the absence of such records is not confirmation of safety; treat custody and out-of-town facility access as open questions rather than settled ones.

regions.name: Schaffhausen
regions.merged_summary: Schaffhausen operates under Switzerland's national regime in full, with no local exception. This small, mostly German-speaking canton on the Rhine near the German border, roughly half an hour from Zurich, is comparatively rural and small-town outside the city of Schaffhausen, with a tourist economy centred on the Rhine Falls and a somewhat more conservative, less cosmopolitan social setting than Zurich or Geneva. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Schaffhausen from the national picture: there is no documented cantonal ordinance, custody provision, border or facility practice singling out trans visitors, and local administration, police and courts function routinely. Everyday friction — staring or awkwardness in a less gender-diverse environment — is more likely than institutional hostility, though the absence of local documentation should not be read as proof that such exposures cannot occur.

regions.name: Solothurn
regions.merged_summary: Solothurn operates under Switzerland's national framework in full, with no cantonal exception documented. The canton is small and German-speaking, combining a mid-sized urban belt around Solothurn and Olten with a more rural, traditionally Catholic-conservative hinterland; its historic old town draws steady tourism, while smaller settlements see far fewer foreign visitors. Local observations describe gender diversity as less familiar here than in Zurich or Basel, so staring, curiosity, misgendering and awkward service encounters are plausible, and specialist trans services are thinner than in the larger centres — scale, rather than organised hostility, is the main local difference. There is no Solothurn-specific legislation either protecting or targeting gender-variant people, and no documented pattern of anti-trans policing, facility restrictions or targeted incidents in the canton. Cantonal police, hospitals, hotels and courts operate under ordinary Swiss rule-of-law conditions, and recourse through them remains available when friction occurs. Detention placement is a cantonal matter: Solothurn has no gender-identity provision comparable to Basel-Stadt's, so a detained visitor's placement would follow general cantonal practice with no documented trans-specific protocol — an open question rather than a demonstrated everyday exposure. Gender-marker mismatches can still prompt bureaucratic questioning at routine document checks, an inconvenience rather than a legal obstacle.

regions.name: St. Gallen
regions.merged_summary: St. Gallen is subject to Switzerland's national regime in full, with no cantonal exception. The canton lies in the German-speaking east, is partly rural and historically Catholic, and leans more socially conservative than Zurich or Geneva, with stronger results for right-leaning parties. Everyday attitudes outside the city of St. Gallen may be less affirming: staring, awkwardness or misgendering are the realistic friction points for an outed trans visitor, particularly in rural districts, rather than a documented hostile institutional pathway. Trans-competent care, community support and visible LGBTQ infrastructure are concentrated in the city of St. Gallen itself and are thinner in the surrounding rural areas; tourism-facing services in the canton are accustomed to foreign visitors. No cantonal restriction on facilities, entry or medical care, no cantonal ban, no police campaign and no record of violence targeting trans people are documented here, and Swiss police and courts remain available for remedy. Detention placement in the canton follows general practice: St. Gallen's detention law carries no explicit gender-identity clause of the kind Basel-Stadt adopted in 2019, so any custody or hospitalisation question rests on how officials apply the ordinary separation rules case by case — an open point rather than a documented harm. The local record shows no pattern of police targeting of trans visitors, but it also contains little canton-specific detail on how bias incidents are handled in practice.

regions.name: Thurgau
regions.merged_summary: Thurgau is subject to Switzerland's national legal framework in full, with no cantonal exception to it. A German-speaking, largely rural canton in eastern Switzerland, it is smaller and more small-town in character than Zurich, Basel or Geneva, centred on Frauenfeld and the Lake Constance shore. The canton has added no trans-specific protections of its own: it has no cantonal detention provision requiring that a detainee's gender identity be respected, and no cantonal conversion-therapy ban, so custody placement and facility use rest on general cantonal practice and staff discretion rather than written trans-sensitive rules; inpatient gender accommodation is likewise less explicit than in cantons with such rules. Social conditions rather than state hostility are the main local variable. The electorate is socially conservative with a religious-conservative streak, and trans community organisations and specialist gender-affirming services are thinner locally than in the major cities, so awkwardness, staring, misgendering or cautious bureaucratic treatment are likelier outcomes of visibility than active protection — particularly outside Frauenfeld and the Lake Constance tourist areas. Courts and authorities function, and no pattern of trans-specific violence, police targeting or organised hostility toward visitors is documented for the canton. For a trans visitor this reads as modestly below the national baseline: friction of social unfamiliarity and inconsistent service interactions rather than legal jeopardy, with detention or inpatient care the residual exposure where local discretion governs.

regions.name: Ticino
regions.merged_summary:
Ticino is subject to Switzerland's national regime on legal gender recognition, partnership and protection from discrimination in full, with no cantonal exception of its own.

Ticino is Switzerland's Italian-speaking southern canton, a tourism and cross-border economy centred on Lugano, Locarno and the lakeside resorts. No cantonal law criminalising transgender identity or expression, restricting access to facilities, or imposing Ticino-specific border or document checks on visitors is known, and no anti-trans incidents specific to the canton are documented. Locally the canton reads as more Catholic and socially conservative than the large German-speaking urban centres, with stronger right-populist currents, particularly outside Lugano and in the rural mountain valleys; support for marriage equality at the ballot was weaker than the Swiss average. In practice this surfaces as friction rather than threat: a trans visitor who is read or outed may meet staring, intrusive questioning, misgendering or occasional hesitation from staff in smaller communities, while Lugano and the main tourist areas are comparatively cosmopolitan. Police and courts function predictably, and identity documents are accepted routinely in ordinary travel and services. One gap worth noting: Ticino's detention legislation contains no explicit gender-identity clause, so how a detained visitor would be placed is not documented, making custody the least certain scenario.

regions.name: Valais
regions.merged_summary: Valais is subject to Switzerland's national legal framework in full, and it is one of the cantons that has already adopted its own ban on conversion therapy. The canton is largely rural and French-speaking with a historically Catholic character, and its social tone outside the main population centres is more conservative than in Zurich or Geneva. In small communes an outed trans visitor is more likely to meet staring, misgendering, curious questioning or mild service friction than hostility; there is no documented pattern of police targeting, organised violence, or any Valais-specific restriction on trans visitors' documents, identity checks or facilities. The major ski and lakeside resorts — Zermatt, Verbier, Crans-Montana — are cosmopolitan and used to international guests, so everyday exposure there is low, while the visible local LGBTQ community is small and concentrated mainly in Sion, Martigny and Monthey. Detainee placement is a cantonal matter, and no gender-identity custody clause is on the record for Valais, leaving emergency custody or hospital placement an open question rather than a known exposure. Local facility practice and visitor-specific incident rates are likewise undocumented, so that uncertainty — not assumed safety — should guide planning.

regions.name: Vaud
regions.merged_summary: Vaud is subject to Switzerland's national regime in full, with no cantonal exception to it. The canton is French-speaking and centred on Lausanne, a large, internationally oriented and comparatively socially liberal city with established LGBTQ+ associations — Dialogai, the long-running Geneva-based helpline and advice service, operates regionally — plus visible queer infrastructure, hotels, clinics, transport and nightlife that generally handle a mismatch between documents and presentation without serious consequence. Vaud is among the more progressive cantons: it enacted a cantonal ban on conversion practices in force since 2024, which signals institutional respect for gender identity rather than a direct traveller safeguard, and cantonal authorities generally treat anti-LGBTIQ+ violence as a policing priority, with police, hospitals and courts functioning under stable rule of law. Outside Lausanne, rural Vaud and small towns are more socially conservative, and everyday exposure for a trans visitor is more likely to be social friction — misgendering, curiosity, awkwardness at document checks, bureaucratic misunderstanding or isolated harassment — than organised state targeting. No Vaud-specific rule governing placement of trans detainees is documented, and no cantonal traveller-facing exclusion campaign or hostile policing aimed at trans visitors is recorded. Trans-specific visitor incidents and local enforcement outcomes in Vaud are not documented, so their absence should not be read as proof of safety; legal clarity in the canton does not by itself prevent hostility or friction in practice.

regions.name: Zug
regions.merged_summary:
Zug is a small, wealthy German-speaking canton built around a compact lakeside business city, with a large international and expatriate population, low street crime and professional policing. The region is subject to Switzerland's national law in full, with no local exception.

Locally the canton is traditionally Catholic, small-town and more socially reserved than Zurich or Geneva, and it has no prominent LGBTQ scene: a trans visitor who is read as trans is more likely to meet curiosity, misgendering or conservative disapproval than official hostility, with social friction rather than police attention the usual outcome of being recognised. No Zug-specific border, facility or public-accommodation ban, trans-specific police targeting, service refusal or hostile local ordinance is documented. Detention placement is decided cantonally, and no Zug rule explicitly respecting a detainee's gender identity is on record, so custody placement is an open question rather than a documented exposure — that absence of local evidence is not itself evidence of safety, and Zug-specific police, hospital-ward and detention practices are simply not documented. Trans-specific healthcare and community infrastructure are thinner in the canton and are often accessed in Zurich. Zug's own position on conversion therapy is likewise not documented either way.

regions.name: Hubei Province
regions.merged_summary: Hubei Province is subject to China's national law in full, with no local exception. No province-level evidence was found that distinguishes Hubei, including Wuhan, from the national picture in terms of official treatment, local enforcement, or protective measures, and no local protections or harsher local measures are known. Hubei is a central, largely conservative province, and Wuhan's size and university population have historically supported a small, visible queer scene — but visitors should expect the same conditions documented at national level, and urban anonymity offers little practical protection if they are outed or questioned.

regions.name: Ningxia Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region
regions.merged_summary: Ningxia is subject to China's national law in full, with no local exception. Beyond that national picture, this Hui-majority autonomous region in the northwest is socially conservative and tightly communal, with stronger ethnic and religious gender-norm expectations, little visible queer subculture and fewer tourism-facing equality norms than coastal cities. Yinchuan's relative urbanism offers some anonymity and more routine travel than the region's smaller cities and towns, where communal scrutiny makes being outed more socially exposing; the local religious and communal context adds disapproval rather than any distinct legal penalty. Local capacity for respectful medical or security handling is limited, and complaints infrastructure is thinner than in coastal centres. Visitors should expect stares, intrusive questioning, possible police stops, difficulty finding trans-friendly services, and refusal or awkward placement in facilities, with little recourse if treated as fraud or disorder. No local protective ordinances, local hostility incidents or organized anti-trans enforcement specific to Ningxia have been documented — that absence should be read as thinner evidence, not as safety. No credible pathway to imprisonment exists here for gender presentation, but discretion remains the practical safeguard.

regions.name: Qinghai Province
regions.merged_summary: Qinghai is subject to China's national law in full, with no local exception. Provincial conditions shape how that regime reaches a trans visitor. Qinghai is a sparsely populated, largely rural western province of Han, Tibetan, Hui and Mongol communities, socially conservative in both Tibetan and Hui areas; Xining, the capital, is comparatively conservative and low-visibility even by national standards. The province has almost no visible queer community or advocacy infrastructure and no trans-specific health or support services outside Xining, so a gender-nonconforming visitor can expect more staring and social friction in smaller towns and religiously observant areas, where being outed makes them highly conspicuous and where refusal of accommodation or services, public disapproval and unsympathetic police handling are plausible. Xining offers more anonymity but little local expertise. Official encounters at hotels, checkpoints, clinics and with police can involve mocking or invasive questioning, and there is little local advocacy presence to intervene if service refusal or policing goes badly. No Qinghai-specific statute, enforcement campaign, protective exception or pattern of organised anti-trans targeting is documented, and general policing appears routine rather than identity-targeted. Accounts differ on the local tourism economy: tourism around Qinghai Lake favours ordinary visitor treatment, while the province as a whole has little tourism that might temper official conduct toward a visibly trans traveller. The risk here is social and bureaucratic rather than a distinct criminal campaign.

regions.name: Shandong Province
regions.merged_summary:
Shandong Province is subject to China's national law in full, with no local exception.

A populous eastern province with a Confucian tradition and comparatively traditional gender norms, Shandong has no region-specific protections, sanctuary practices or documented local exceptions, and no patterned or organized violence against trans people has been recorded here. Everyday exposure is shaped by routine document and police ID checks in Jinan, Qingdao and at tourist sites such as Mount Tai, where hotels and attractions register guests against passport details. Qingdao's tourism character and the student districts of Jinan and Qingdao offer some urban anonymity, and foreign visitors' paperwork at hotels and attractions tends to attract less attention than it might elsewhere — this softens appearance only and does not offset the absence of recourse. Outside those areas gender-nonconforming visibility is low, and queer social infrastructure is thin province-wide. A visibly trans visitor should expect stares, intrusive questions and service friction, and where police, medical or family involvement arises, handling that defaults to documents and birth sex — with misgendering, contact with relatives or employers, and possible psychiatric or family intervention rather than respectful accommodation. Enforcement a visitor encounters is likely to be administrative rather than custodial, but discovery would bring humiliation or service denial rather than institutional protection.

regions.name: Taiwan Province
regions.merged_summary:
Taiwan Province is administered under its own constitution, courts and immigration system, so the PRC national regime described at country level does not apply there.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised since 2019, and statutory protections against gender-identity discrimination cover employment and education, with administrative courts and gender-equality bodies available for complaints. Gender-marker changes on identity documents have been available without mandatory surgery following a series of 2021–2023 administrative and court decisions, though some legal pathways still seek medical proof, and foreign passports are generally respected as presented. Gender-affirming medical care is available through established clinics. Taipei hosts large public Pride events with official tolerance, an openly visible trans community, and police and courts that handle LGBT complaints as routine business.

Friction is chiefly social and bureaucratic. Expect staring, misgendering and occasional awkward handling where documents do not match presentation — at hotels, clinics or other private services — with attitudes less forgiving in rural areas and among older generations, and coverage in housing and everyday services thinner than in the capital. Gender-segregated facilities, including hospital wards and any detention setting, may be assigned by registered sex, and practice here is uneven. Border handling of visibly trans visitors shows no documented pattern of targeting, but visitor-specific evidence on facility access, healthcare and document mismatches is limited, so these remain open questions rather than established exposures. A traveller whose itinerary continues into mainland China remains subject to PRC exit and document rules there.

regions.name: Bas-Sassandra
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Côte d'Ivoire's national law in full, with no local exception. Bas-Sassandra is a southwestern coastal and agricultural region centred on San-Pédro, and its port and the beach areas around Jacqueville draw visitors and some tourist-facing tolerance, while interior forest districts are more socially conservative and further from functioning complaint mechanisms. Compared with Abidjan, the region is less cosmopolitan, with fewer services, thinner trans-specific support and advocacy infrastructure, and less anonymity: in smaller towns and farming communities, discovery is harder to avoid and relocation or assistance is less available. A visitor who is outed in a smaller city or beach town could expect staring, gossip, refusal of services and discretionary police attention, and smaller communities and local conservatism can make such confrontation more likely. Tourism and routine discretion may soften day-to-day encounters, but they do not alter the underlying environment. No local protective exception, organised targeting specific to Bas-Sassandra, or effective local protective recourse has been documented, so the inherited national exposure governs, with somewhat thinner recourse outside Abidjan.

regions.name: Lagunes
regions.merged_summary:
Lagunes is the southern district containing Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire's largest city and main economic hub, and the region is subject to the national regime in full with no local exception.

Abidjan is cosmopolitan, with a functioning hotel and hospitality sector and an active human-rights community, and the anonymity of a large city offers some cover for a trans visitor. At the same time, most of the country's documented anti-LGBTQ violence and enforcement is concentrated in this region rather than spread evenly nationwide: recorded raids on venues frequented by gender-nonconforming people, street assaults and extortion aimed at feminine-presenting trans women, and a sharp late-2024 spike in assaults all sit here, and feminine-presenting trans women remain the most exposed group locally. No Lagunes-specific protective exception, improved enforcement practice or harsher authority has been identified; discovery can still bring harassment, assault, extortion or short detention.

Nothing has been documented locally on border checks, visitor facilities, custody rules or health-care access for trans travellers. That silence reflects a lack of evidence rather than safety, and neither the city's tourism profile nor its proximity to the capital guarantees protection.

regions.name: Valle Du Bandama
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Côte d'Ivoire's national law in full, with no local exception. Bouaké, the regional centre, is a conservative interior city with a heavy security presence and little in the way of queer support services or tourist infrastructure, leaving a trans visitor with less anonymity and thinner recourse than in Abidjan. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Valle Du Bandama from the national picture, and the absence of local incident reports should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Centre
regions.merged_summary:
The Centre Region is Cameroon's political capital: Yaoundé houses the presidency, the courts, the gendarmerie and police high commands, and a dense network of checkpoints and identity controls. A visibly gender-nonconforming visitor moving through the capital meets a heavier concentration of official scrutiny than in other regions — routine document checks, stops and questioning, and a greater chance that appearance alone draws attention from security personnel. Social attitudes in the city are conservative and official-facing, and state-controlled media are concentrated here, so exposure carries a real risk of public outing.

The region is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. Documented appearance-based prosecutions have run through Yaoundé's courts, including a 2011 case of people jailed for wearing women's clothing and the case of Jean-Claude Roger Mbede, whose sentencing proceeded through Kondengui Central Prison in the capital; an appeals court here has overturned a comparable appearance-based conviction, so appeal is possible though not dependable. Custody after an arrest in the capital would most likely be at Kondengui, where conditions for detainees held on such grounds are described as harsh. Yaoundé's large diplomatic, expatriate and NGO presence and its urban anonymity offer some practical cover and modestly better access to consular and legal contact than elsewhere in the country, but they do not shield a visitor from state scrutiny once noticed, and no local protective measure, tolerance or enforcement exception is known here.

regions.name: Far North
regions.merged_summary: The Far North is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. It is the country's most socially conservative region: predominantly Muslim, largely rural, and bordering Nigeria and Chad, with customary and religious authorities carrying strong weight in public morality and tight community scrutiny of outsiders. Small towns such as Maroua and the settlements around the Lake Chad basin offer little anonymity, and outside Waza National Park tourism is minimal, so a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor stands out quickly. Security is militarised: frequent army and gendarmerie checkpoints, armed-community vigilance and displacement linked to the Boko Haram insurgency mean encounters with officialdom are more common than in the south, while state presence and rule of law are weaker and further reduced by recent insurgency-related insecurity. There is no local LGBTQ support organisation, no visible trans community infrastructure, and markedly fewer willing defence lawyers and accessible courts than in Douala or Yaoundé, so detention, coercive questioning, extortion and hostility from civilians or armed groups are realistic local outcomes, and routes to release, appeal or outside help are slower from remote districts. No local protections, documented tolerance or region-specific prosecutions are on record here; the absence of regional case detail reflects thin reporting rather than safer conditions, and it should not be read as reassurance. Where local conditions meet the national framework, they intensify exposure rather than soften it: deeper conservatism, low anonymity and heavy surveillance make discovery more likely to escalate, with thinner institutional recourse once it happens.

regions.name: Littoral
regions.merged_summary: Littoral is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. Douala, the economic capital and main port, is a large, commercially dense and cosmopolitan city where a trans visitor can draw on port traffic, business travel and expatriate mobility for anonymity, and where consular and NGO contacts are within reach. That cover lasts only until an official encounter: routine police checks in a busy port setting mean documents or gender presentation can attract attention, and Littoral's own courts have heard the country's most prominent appearance-based prosecutions of trans people. Practical help once things go wrong is thin — support infrastructure in the region has been disrupted by police action, and lawyers willing to take such cases are scarce — while reporting from the region describes arbitrary detention, beatings of detainees and group attacks following allegations of gender nonconformity. Nothing local offsets the national exposure: the city's scale makes casual recognition less likely and offers modest informal cover, but it does not soften the state's response once someone is outed, and detention in the region carries little recourse.

regions.name: South-West
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception.

What distinguishes the South-West is its security environment rather than any local variant of that law. The Anglophone conflict since 2016–2017 has concentrated military and gendarmerie checkpoints along roads around Buea, Limbe and Kumba, alongside separatist-imposed curfews and 'ghost-town' lockdowns, stop-and-search and routine identity checks by both state forces and armed separatist groups, which operate with practical impunity in places. Beating and unrecorded detention in security custody are live risks there, and a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor's documents are more likely to be examined and any subsequent detention to disappear from view. Policing, courts and legal aid are weaker than in Douala or Yaoundé, with fewer functioning lawyers, courts and advocacy groups available after an arrest, and improvised routes around checkpoints are difficult.

Local social conditions cut both ways. Attitudes in the South-West are broadly conservative, more so than on the francophone coast, while Limbe's coastal tourist economy, the Mount Cameroon area and Buea's university population bring some familiarity with foreign visitors. Neither offers a documented exception to national enforcement practice: no trans-specific local protection, support organisation or protective machinery is known anywhere in the region, and no distinct local pattern of anti-trans targeting has been established either. Border treatment of foreign documents, facility access and placement in custody are likewise not specifically documented for the region, and that uncertainty should not be read as safety.

regions.name: West
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Cameroon's national law in full, with no local exception. The West Region centres on Bafoussam and the Bamiléké highlands: a predominantly Francophone, strongly Christian and traditional area of close-knit, chieftaincy-organised communities where anonymity is limited in the smaller cities and towns. Local policing, prosecution and court practice follow the national pattern, and no local protective practice, safe-enclave tolerance or tourist-facing leniency is documented. Outside Douala and Yaoundé, legal aid, media scrutiny and support networks are thinner: no LGBTQ organisation or dedicated legal service is known to operate here, and few lawyers are willing to take such cases. Discovery is likely to involve family, community elders or local authorities as a matter of public morality rather than a private dispute, so exposure tends to become public and reputationally damaging before any official encounter. A trans visitor whose presentation is questioned can expect detention, extortion, misgendering in custody and public hostility, with minimal recourse; foreign visitors carry passport documents that will be checked on any police contact. No region-specific case of a trans person prosecuted or shielded in the West is on record — a silence that reflects the lack of local reporting and support infrastructure rather than any demonstrated local safety, leaving a visitor isolated if something goes wrong.

regions.name: Central Kasai
regions.merged_summary: Central Kasai is subject to DR Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a largely rural, inland region centred on Kananga, with very little foreign tourism, no LGBT community infrastructure, and no trans-specific shelter, protection protocol or traveller-facing safeguard known to exist. Strong customary and church authority shapes public life here, and church groups press a view of homosexuality as immoral in a deeply Christian, socially conservative interior where a foreigner's gender presentation draws attention rather than deference. The Kamuina Nsapu conflict of 2016–2019 left security-force abuses, displacement and damaged courts in Kasaï Central, and state institutions remain thinner than in Kinshasa or Lubumbashi. That legacy is a dated warning about protection and accountability rather than evidence of a current campaign targeting trans people; unlike eastern DRC, no armed-group control is documented locally, but police discretion remains broad and ordinary state presence is weaker than in the capital, so consular or judicial recourse after an incident would be doubtful. In practice, discovery of a trans visitor's identity would most plausibly bring police or militia attention rather than a working remedy: locally reported patterns include questioning, extortion, arbitrary detention, social or family exposure, denial or abuse of care, and violence by non-state actors, with near-total impunity. Custody or hospital placement would follow birth sex and could itself expose a trans visitor to harm. Nothing local indicates safer treatment than the national pattern, and no tourist-facing mitigations exist.

regions.name: Haut-Katanga
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to DR Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. Haut-Katanga is the copper-mining southeast of the country, centred on Lubumbashi near the Zambian border — a large commercial and expatriate hub whose urban scale and foreign mining presence give a trans visitor somewhat more anonymity than rural areas. Unlike the eastern provinces, the province is not under armed-militia control, so the extreme non-state violence recorded elsewhere in DRC does not operate here; the actors most likely to matter are the national police and courts, whose checkpoint scrutiny, routine stops, extortion and harassment apply throughout the territory, and Katanga has its own record of political violence and security-force action. Provincial society is strongly church-influenced and Christian-majority, with church groups publicly opposing homosexuality. Police stops, hotel or border document checks and hospital admission are the points where a mismatch between presentation and documents tends to surface, and discovery can bring detention in facilities assigned by birth sex, with no effective recourse documented for detention, harassment or assault. Outside Lubumbashi, state administration is thinner and extraction areas carry some armed-actor presence. No region-specific protections, police training, inclusive facilities, community infrastructure or trans-specific case records are documented for the province, and the city's foreign economic presence does not by itself guarantee safe entry, medical care or detention treatment.

regions.name: Haut-Lomami
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception.

Haut-Lomami is a large, sparsely populated rural province — the former Katanga territory centred on Kamina, with Kamina, Bukama and Lubudi as its main settlements — and has very limited tourism, a thin judicial presence and little oversight. It lies outside the eastern belt where the worst documented militia violence occurs, but it is a deeply conservative area where Christian church teaching dominates social norms and LGBTQ visibility is low, so a visibly trans visitor stands out in its small communities; the anonymity available in a city such as Kinshasa does not extend here.

State reach is thin outside Kamina. The province's rural transport corridor and its military and security checkpoints mean inconsistent identity documents are noticed easily, and a routine document check or dispute can escalate into arbitrary detention, extortion or public humiliation with little realistic recourse. No local trans community, advocacy group or protective service is known to be available if a visitor is outed, and remedies are constrained by the province's sparse courts. Travelling the corridor alone or with a child raises exposure to official encounters and to armed criminal actors operating with limited accountability.

regions.name: Kasai
regions.merged_summary:
Kasai is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception.

Centred on Kananga and Mbuji-Mayi, the region is socially conservative and strongly shaped by Catholic and evangelical churches that frame homosexuality and gender diversity as immoral; customary chiefs hold sway, and there is no trans community infrastructure — no dedicated shelter, legal-aid network or protective organisation is known. Foreign visitors stand out, and the region sees little tourism, so visible gender nonconformity tends to be noticed. Discovery could bring humiliation, extortion, service refusal, questioning or arbitrary detention, particularly away from the main urban centres.

Security conditions carry a mixed picture. The 2016–2017 Kamuina Nsapu conflict left documented abuses by army forces and militias, mass graves and weakened state authority across Kasai-Oriental and Kasai-Central, and routine checkpoints, hospitals, courts and police stations can be unreliable or dangerous; some assessments note that Kasai sees less armed-group predation than the east and that provincial administration is more present, which narrows the impunity risk slightly without eliminating it. Consular and legal help is distant, and no local tolerance or protective exception distinguishes the region from the national picture. Exact enforcement against trans foreigners is poorly documented, and no region-specific records of trans-specific enforcement or facility rules were found — a gap that does not establish safety. Discretion about identity documents, gender presentation and public visibility remains advisable throughout.

regions.name: Kongo-Central
regions.merged_summary:
Kongo-Central is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception.

The province is the country's only coastal one, built around the seaport of Matadi — DR Congo's principal port — the deepwater terminal at Banana, and the towns of Boma, Muanda and Kisantu. Unlike the eastern provinces it has no armed-group or militia presence; police, courts and a functioning provincial administration are in place instead, so the practical exposure for a trans visitor comes from official encounters rather than militia predation. Ports, roads and the land borders with Angola and the Republic of Congo are lined with checkpoints, where a mismatch between documents and presentation is more likely to draw attention, and foreign visitors stand out outside Matadi and Muanda, leaving thin anonymity outside the larger towns.

Socially the province is strongly conservative and church-dominated, with a Bakongo moralist movement active around Matadi. Policing is uneven and at times corrupt, and no local protections, complaint mechanisms, trans-specific services or tourism-facing safeguards are known. The absence of reported Kongo-Central incidents is thin evidence rather than safety: nothing in the local record suggests better document handling, policing or social acceptance here than the national picture, and a visitor outed as trans would likely find little practical recourse.

regions.name: Kwango
regions.merged_summary: Kwango lies in south-western DR Congo and is subject to the national regime in full, with no local exception. The province is predominantly rural, with limited tourism and sparse hospitals, legal aid and advocacy infrastructure; no trans or LGBTQ organisation, shelter, specialist legal aid service or reliable complaint mechanism is known to operate, and realistic remedies lie far from most settlements. Customary chiefs and church authorities shape everyday moral enforcement, and church-based moral hostility is strong. Dense small-town social networks mean that a visitor outed in the provincial capital Kenge or in a smaller settlement would face exposure to non-professional local actors first, with discovery spreading quickly. Plausible local outcomes include stigma, community harassment, extortion, arbitrary questioning and short detention, with state institutions having limited reach beyond the main town, weak rule of law and little police accountability; security-force involvement remains possible while protection is uncertain. Kwango is distant from the eastern areas where armed-militia violence against LGBTQ people is reported, and no organised anti-trans campaign is documented here — but the local record is thin, and the absence of documented incidents in a poorly documented interior province is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Kwilu
regions.merged_summary: Kwilu, a largely rural western province centred on Kikwit, is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Kwilu from the national picture: there are no documented local protections, no locally distinct enforcement practice, and no tourism-facing tolerance known to exist there, and the absence of local reports should not be read as safety. What can be said of the province itself is that it is inland, church-influenced and thinly touristed, with less visitor-facing infrastructure and far less legal, medical or civil-society support than Kinshasa, so a trans visitor who becomes visible — at accommodation, a checkpoint or a police stop — has fewer places to turn and thinner practical recourse. How identity documents issued abroad are handled locally is uncertain, and the practical consequences of any encounter fall back on the national framework.

regions.name: Lomami
regions.merged_summary:
Lomami is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a poor, landlocked interior region centred on Kabinda with limited transport links, no tourist-facing economy and very few foreign visitors. State presence is thin: policing is poorly resourced, extortion is routine, courts and legal aid are effectively absent outside the main towns, and customary and church authorities carry strong weight in a deeply conservative social climate.

In small-town Lomami, anonymity is hard to keep — a trans visitor who is discovered becomes known quickly, with no community infrastructure, specialist services or discreet urban refuge to fall back on. Official encounters carry a real risk of arbitrary questioning, detention, extortion or assault, and any detention would place you by birth sex. Redress is essentially unavailable: no local remedy, legal aid or protective service is documented, and the practical conditions for seeking help are materially worse than in Kinshasa. Church-led moral opposition is prominent, so social consequences can compound official ones.

Militia violence against LGBTQ people is documented elsewhere in DR Congo but is not specifically recorded for Lomami; that silence reflects thin documentation rather than established local safety, and the fragility of state authority in the interior means a serious incident would be unlikely to be investigated. No local tolerance, trans-specific policy or protective layer is known to distinguish the province from the national picture.

regions.name: Lualaba
regions.merged_summary: Lualaba is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a comparatively stable mining region in the south-eastern interior centred on Kolwezi, with the Zambian border corridor at Kasumbalesa carrying steady cross-border traffic. Unlike the eastern provinces it is not under armed-militia control, so that exposure documented elsewhere in the country does not apply here; what remains locally is state-actor risk and social stigma. In practice, checkpoints, hotels, and mining-company or expatriate services are the settings where a mismatch between a visitor's presentation and their papers is most likely to be noticed. Church-led moral disapproval is widespread and rule of law is weak, so recourse for a foreign trans visitor who is outed is thin. Kolwezi's commercial and expatriate traffic does, however, make foreign visitors comparatively unremarkable. No local protection, local tolerance, or trans-targeting pattern has been recorded for Lualaba, so conditions here remain uncertain rather than demonstrably safe, and nothing local is protective.

regions.name: Tanganyika
regions.merged_summary: Tanganyika is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception. The province lies around Lake Tanganyika with its capital at Kalemie, a remote lakeside mining area with limited tourism and urban services, conservative church-influenced social norms, and weaker courts and oversight than in Kinshasa. It borders South Kivu and has seen sustained intercommunal conflict, Mai-Mai militia activity and large-scale displacement, leaving state authority uneven and checkpoints predatory, though it has not experienced the extreme militia campaigns reported further east. For a trans visitor, being discovered in hotels, on transport, or during encounters with police and armed actors risks arbitrary questioning, detention, extortion or assault, with accountability and protection limited and little realistic recourse. No trans-specific services, advocacy, anti-discrimination enforcement, approachable policing or documented social tolerance is known for the province, and the absence of such reports is not assurance of safety. Local instability and conservative norms add exposure rather than offsetting it, so discretion and a low profile remain advisable.

regions.name: Upper Uele
regions.merged_summary: Upper Uele is subject to DR Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. Upper Uele (Haut-Uele) is a remote, sparsely populated province in the north-east centred on Isiro, with poor infrastructure, very limited tourism and thin state presence; police, courts and services are weak across much of the province, so security falls largely to police, army units and local armed actors. Armed groups operate in parts of the wider north-east with little accountability, though the province sits outside eastern DRC's militia belt and no province-specific campaign against LGBTQ people is documented. Public culture is strongly influenced by churches that frame homosexuality as immoral, and there is no known LGBTQ organisation, safe venue, visible trans community or local protective policy to offset the national regime. A trans visitor who is discovered — at a checkpoint, a guesthouse or a clinic — may face hostility, extortion, arbitrary detention, denial of accommodation or care, or mob hostility, with officials operating with little accountability and hospitals and consular help distant. That no trans-specific rule or incident is documented here is a gap in evidence, not evidence of safety, and no region-specific mitigation for travellers is known.

regions.name: Équateur
regions.merged_summary:
Équateur is a remote northwestern province centred on the Congo River port of Mbandaka, one of the least-governed parts of the country, with very few foreign visitors, thin infrastructure and no tourism economy to speak of. The region is subject to DR Congo national law in full, with no local exception.

Outside Mbandaka, police, courts and legal aid function weakly, medical infrastructure is limited, and nothing documented locally softens national practice for a trans visitor: there are no known protective services, no local tolerance and no trans community infrastructure to turn to. Police and officials are underpaid and resort to extortion, so an outed visitor could face detention, humiliation, coerced disclosure, denial of care or violence with effectively no working recourse. Church and customary authority shape strong social disapproval; a travelling minor could additionally face family or community "correction" or state inquiry.

Unlike the conflict-affected east, no armed-group campaign against LGBTQ people is documented in Équateur, but weak state presence leaves poorly controlled security personnel as the practical exposure rather than militia. Document checks at river and air transport points can draw attention to papers or presentation, and riverine and rural isolation makes a discreet exit difficult once questions arise. How national provisions are applied to trans visitors specifically is uncertain, and no Équateur-specific protective measures or reliable visitor remedies are established.

regions.name: Bouenza
regions.merged_summary: Bouenza is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. The department is largely rural and administrative, centred on Madingou, with minimal foreign tourism and fewer of the legal-aid and civil-society services concentrated in Brazzaville, so a trans visitor stands out more in close-knit settings and has less anonymity and less access to support than in the capital. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Bouenza's treatment of a trans visitor from the national picture: local enforcement, visitor experiences, and local attitudes are not documented here, and the lack of recorded incidents in the department should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Cuvette
regions.merged_summary: Cuvette is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. The department is a largely rural interior region centred on Owando, with small towns such as Oyo and Boundji and long distances from Brazzaville. Police and court presence is thin, oversight is limited, and there are no LGBTQI+ or trans organisations, no support network, and scarce medical and legal services — so a trans visitor's practical protection is weaker than national texts alone suggest. A visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor has little anonymity in small administrative centres: in tightly knit households and villages, discovery is more likely to surface as kin and neighbour pressure, harassment or intrusive questioning than as a discreet private matter. Any official encounter — over mismatched documents or presentation — occurs far from oversight, and reporting is rare where the infrastructure for it is thinnest. Realistically, recourse after an incident would mean travelling to Brazzaville or leaving the country; there is no documented Cuvette-specific anti-trans travel regime or organised detention, but local practice has not been documented in enough detail to treat that absence as reassurance. Social conservatism in the interior appears at least as strong as in the capital, though the available attitude evidence comes from Brazzaville and should not be assumed to describe Cuvette. No separate regional law or protective regime distinguishes Cuvette from the national picture, and no local incidents are documented.

regions.name: Cuvette-Ouest
regions.merged_summary: Cuvette-Ouest is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a remote, sparsely populated northwestern department centred on Owando, far from the institutions of Brazzaville, predominantly rural and under-resourced, with eco-tourism around Odzala-Kokoua offering the main international-facing presence and few formal complaint channels in everyday life. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes how this department treats a trans visitor from the national picture; visitors should therefore assume conditions match those described at country level, and the lack of local documentation should not be read as safer.

regions.name: Kouilou
regions.merged_summary: Kouilou falls under the national regime of the Republic of the Congo in full, with no local legal exception. Kouilou is the country's coastal department, centred on Pointe-Noire, the economic and oil capital and main port; its oil-services, port and beach-and-lodge tourism economy (including Loango) draws a more cosmopolitan, foreign-accustomed population than the interior, and hotel and clinic encounters in urban tourist-facing districts tend to be formalised. That anonymity is uneven: outside the Pointe-Noire orbit the department is small and tight-knit, with limited anonymity, thin legal and NGO support, and a visibly trans visitor likely to be read as foreign and unusual, drawing scrutiny, service friction or extortion attempts rather than organised state targeting. Airport and port checks and other bureaucratic encounters are where document-and-presentation mismatches most plausibly surface, and beyond them no effective local remedy is documented. Police extortion dynamics and family- and community-driven hostility operate much as they do nationally. No Kouilou-specific legislation, facility bans, custody rules, protective ordinance, enforcement record or community infrastructure is known either way — an absence of local evidence, not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Likouala
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception.

Likouala is a remote, densely forested and sparsely populated northern department centred on Impfondo, with negligible tourism infrastructure and no known LGBTQ community presence or trans-support organisation. State presence is thin: police, health and judicial services are limited and far apart, while customary and religious authority carries more weight than in Brazzaville. Communities are close-knit and strongly conservative, so a trans visitor who is outed may find word spreading quickly among neighbours, clinic staff and local officers, while practical remedies — complaint routes, trans-aware medical or legal help — are largely unavailable. There is no known local record either of transgender visitors being specifically targeted or of protective enforcement practice, so conditions on the ground remain uncertain rather than assuredly benign. Daily circumstances cut both ways: sporadic policing and remote checkpoints mean less routine document scrutiny and less surveillance than the capital, but the same remoteness makes extortion, service denial or harassment harder to escape, report or overturn, and any official encounter is likely to be an isolated one with little oversight.

regions.name: Lékoumou
regions.merged_summary: Lékoumou is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. The department is a small, rural area in the country's south-west centred on Sibiti, where tight-knit communities and limited anonymity make a visibly trans visitor relatively easy to notice. No local evidence was found that distinguishes Lékoumou from the national picture: no incidents, enforcement differences, local protections or community organisations specific to trans visitors are documented here, and that silence should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Niari
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Niari's treatment of trans visitors from the national picture, and this absence of local documentation should not be read as a sign of safety. Niari is a largely rural southern department centred on Dolisie along the main Brazzaville–Pointe-Noire road and rail corridor, an urban and transit setting where routine document checks and guesthouse registration can raise exposure to ordinary police encounters.

regions.name: Plateaux
regions.merged_summary: Plateaux is a sparsely populated interior department centred on Djambala, with almost no tourist infrastructure, a customary and church-based social order and thin police presence — conditions that make a visibly transgender visitor conspicuous and leave few local services to turn to. The region is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Plateaux from the national picture on policing, documentation, facilities or recourse, and that lack of local record should not be read as safety: neither added protection nor documented tolerance offsets the national position for a trans visitor.

regions.name: Pool
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to the Republic of the Congo's national law in full, with no local exception. Pool Department wraps around Brazzaville and is largely rural and semi-rural, with lower tourism traffic and far less visible legal, NGO and activist support than the capital. Its security history colours everyday life: a Ninja-militia insurgency ran until the 2017 peace agreement, and rural parts retain thinner police and court presence, so recourse after harassment or extortion is slow and often informal. The Brazzaville–Pointe-Noire corridor crossing the department carries security checkpoints, where document scrutiny is routine and anonymity is limited — a visibly trans or outed visitor may face heightened exposure to extortion, public humiliation or refusal of services, with little practical remedy nearby. Community scrutiny in rural settlements is more conservative than in the capital, and the Brazzaville-facing corridor offers little practical difference from the city itself. Emergency and health infrastructure is limited, adding exposure if care is needed after a disclosure. Violence is not documented as locally organised in Pool, but reporting and protection are weak, and no local protections — nor any locally documented hostility beyond the national picture — have been identified for trans visitors. The absence of such local evidence is not evidence of safety; where local information runs out, national conditions remain the operative baseline.

regions.name: Sangha
regions.merged_summary: Sangha department lies in the far north of the Republic of the Congo and is subject to the national regime in full, with no local exception. It is a sparsely populated, heavily forested frontier along the Sangha river centred on Ouésso, with logging towns and safari lodges serving the Nouabalé-Ndoki area and a border with the Central African Republic that adds customs scrutiny. Police, courts, legal aid, NGOs and official oversight are thin outside Brazzaville and concentrated around Ouésso, and there is no known local trans community or advocacy infrastructure, so an outed visitor has little realistic remedy. In small towns a visibly gender-divergent foreigner is conspicuous; checkpoints and local authorities can bring prolonged questioning, gossip, service refusal and community or family pressure, with conservative rural norms and little outsider familiarity with gender diversity shaping everyday encounters. Tourist-facing accommodation likely cushions routine treatment, but remoteness makes practical assistance harder to reach and weakens institutional checks on misconduct. No region-specific record documents added local protections or a distinct local pattern of trans-related enforcement, and the absence of documented local incidents does not establish safety; what is known locally points to weaker recourse and greater visibility than in the capital.

regions.name: Cook Islands
regions.merged_summary: The Cook Islands is the entire jurisdiction, so a single national legal framework applies across all islands with no subnational variation. Geographically it is a small, tourism-oriented Polynesian archipelago whose economy, centred on Rarotonga, routinely absorbs foreign visitors, and everyday hostility toward trans guests tends to be lower than in less tourism-dependent places. Traditional Cook Islands culture recognises gender-diverse people, referred to locally as akava'ine (with raerae and māhū used in related regional usage), and an established community gives trans visitors a degree of visibility and social acceptance. Against this, churches and family life are broadly conservative Christian, and the small, close-knit society means anonymity is minimal: once known, a visitor's gender history can become common knowledge quickly, with misgendering, curiosity, privacy exposure or disapproval more likely outcomes than state hostility. No trans-specific criminal offence, border or police targeting, facility restriction or pattern of violence against trans visitors is documented — but coverage is thin, so this absence should not be read as proof of safety. Practical protections are limited: there is no local legal gender recognition, no gender-identity anti-discrimination or hate-crime coverage, and facilities and custody arrangements follow birth sex in practice. Gender-affirming healthcare is scarce, service and care continuity can be uneven, and formal recourse through small institutions is thin, with outer islands having fewer services than Rarotonga. Overall, conditions cut both ways — a low general-crime, hospitable, tourism-facing setting alongside church-influenced conservatism where being outed can invite social friction rather than detention.

regions.name: Maio
regions.merged_summary: Maio falls wholly under Cabo Verde's national regime, with no local exception. What distinguishes the island is its scale: a small, quiet, predominantly rural and fishing community of roughly 3,000 residents centred on Vila do Maio (Porto Inglês), with modest tourist infrastructure and none of the anonymity available in Praia or Sal. A gender-nonconforming visitor stands out, and in a tight-knit setting that visibility is likely to turn into sustained curiosity, gossip and public discovery more readily than in larger tourist centres — exposure that is harder to remedy informally. Practical support is thin: policing is light, health and administrative services are limited and may not be trained in transgender-related care, and access to police, media or complaint channels is slower than on bigger islands. There is no visible local trans community and few advocacy or support resources, so friction tends to be social and bureaucratic — a document mismatch drawing attention, an outsider's presentation being questioned — rather than anything recorded as official hostility. No local incidents, ordinances or protections are documented on either side: nothing indicates targeting or detention of trans visitors here, and equally nothing indicates added local safeguards, so the absence of reported problems should not be read as proof of safety. The concerns on Maio are visibility, gossip, uncertain document handling and limited recourse rather than any island-specific penalty.

regions.name: Mosteiros
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception. Mosteiros is a small municipality on Fogo, off the country's main tourist circuits, with a rural, conservative Catholic social texture: a visibly transgender visitor would stand out in a place with limited anonymity and no known trans-specific services or venues. Local conditions — fewer trans-visible public services and less routine familiarity with mismatched travel documents or non-conforming presentation than larger centres — mean that being noticed is likely to feel intrusive, bringing curiosity, gossip, misgendering, awkward scrutiny, bureaucratic questioning, delays and service friction rather than documented official hostility. Police and officials operate under the rule of law but may be unevenly trained in trans issues, so the realistic concern after discovery is social and bureaucratic: confusion, delays and discomfort. No local laws, incidents, raids, custody practices or campaigns targeting gender-nonconforming visitors are documented here, and physical risk appears low; in a small municipality the service and complaint infrastructure is thinner than in the capital, so problems are easier to raise elsewhere than locally.

regions.name: Paul
regions.merged_summary:
Paul falls wholly under Cabo Verde's national regime, with no local exception.

Paul is a small, rural, mountainous municipality with dispersed settlements and low tourism, sitting outside the resort tourism belt of Sal and Boa Vista and seeing far fewer visitors than Praia or Mindelo. In a close-knit community a trans visitor has little anonymity: a document that does not match presentation, visible nonconformity, or being outed is likely to be noticed by neighbours and to draw curiosity, gossip and possible friction in everyday social and accommodation settings rather than organised state action — this is where practical risk concentrates. Local services are thin: medical care, legal assistance and formal complaint or advocacy channels are limited compared with the capital, with less institutional familiarity and slower administrative response, so help is harder to reach if something goes wrong. The record contains no documented pattern of police targeting, sweeps, facility bans, immigration exclusions or trans-specific violence in Paul — but local data is sparse, so that silence reflects thin documentation rather than evidence of safety, and rural conservatism adds uncertainty to an already little-surveyed picture.

regions.name: Porto Novo
regions.merged_summary: Porto Novo is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception. Porto Novo is the main town of Santo Antão, Cabo Verde's most rural large island: a small ferry-port community centred on farming, far less touristed than Praia or Mindelo, where anonymity is limited and a visibly trans visitor is likely to become known quickly in a tight-knit setting. Local medical, legal, lodging and support services are thin, institutions have little everyday experience with transgender identity, and there is no specialised support infrastructure, so practical recourse if a visitor is outed or treated awkwardly at a small hotel, clinic or transport desk is limited. No trans-specific violence, police campaign, morality policing, facility ban or organised targeting is recorded for Porto Novo or elsewhere on the island, and general institutions function. The realistic exposure is social rather than custodial: gossip, curiosity, awkward treatment in small businesses and bureaucratic uncertainty, with little prospect of arrest. The quiet, matter-of-fact tolerance reported elsewhere in Cabo Verde appears to hold here, but that is a national pattern rather than a local guarantee, and thin local evidence should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Ribeira Grande
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception. Ribeira Grande is a small, rural, tight-knit municipality where visible transgender identity is unfamiliar and anonymity is limited, so gossip, curiosity or awkward service encounters are a realistic prospect. Beyond this, no region-specific evidence distinguishes Ribeira Grande from the national picture: local enforcement, service access and the day-to-day treatment of trans visitors are simply not documented for this municipality, and that silence should not be read as reassurance.

regions.name: Ribeira Grande de Santiago
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Cabo Verde's national regime in full, with no local exception. Ribeira Grande de Santiago is a small, largely rural and mountainous municipality on Santiago island, built around the fishing and farming settlements of Cidade Velha — a UNESCO World Heritage site — and lying close to the capital, Praia. Assessments of its character differ: it is described both as having a tourism-facing, relatively cosmopolitan mix near the capital, and as a historic, tightly knit town with limited tourist infrastructure. Local life is more conservative and Catholic than in Praia, with less anonymity for a visibly trans visitor: outsiders stand out, and disapproval, where present, tends to be personal and social rather than organised. The municipality has no dedicated LGBT infrastructure and fewer clinics, legal aid services and visitor resources than the capital, and no local organisation to smooth awkward encounters at a counter or clinic. No trans-specific incident, police targeting or facility ban is documented here. Practical friction — curiosity, misgendering, questions about documents — is the likelier experience than confrontation, and police and court recourse, while available in principle, is untested in this municipality for trans-specific purposes.

regions.name: Santa Catarina
regions.merged_summary:
Santa Catarina is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception. The municipality sits on Santiago, and descriptions of its character vary: some place it as the capital municipality with denser urban services — hospitals, police and consular access — and greater exposure to foreign visitors, while others describe a rural, agricultural community centred on the regional town of Assomada with surrounding farming villages. Either way, it is far less tourist-facing than Praia or the resort islands, with little of the anonymity they offer. No separate local law, protection or documented pattern of trans-specific targeting distinguishes the region from the national picture.

The operative local conditions are social. In small, closely knit communities a trans visitor whose documents and presentation differ should expect close scrutiny, sustained curiosity and gossip, and a real chance of refusal or inconsistent treatment in lodging and services. Informal accommodation of mismatched documents is less likely here than in more tourist-facing places, and no local precedent for such flexibility exists; police and courts function, but officials may be unfamiliar with foreign documents and trans-specific recourse is thin. Trans-specific acceptance is not measured locally, and no pattern of anti-trans violence is documented. The realistic risks after discovery are embarrassment, exclusion or harassment with limited remedies — not state persecution.

regions.name: Santa Catarina do Fogo
regions.merged_summary:
Santa Catarina do Fogo is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception.

The municipality lies inland on Fogo's slopes — a small, largely Catholic and agricultural area whose settlements include Cova Figueira and Chã das Caldeiras — set apart from the island's main visitor traffic through São Filipe. Chã das Caldeiras draws some tourism, giving residents familiarity with foreign travellers, but the communities are tight-knit and low-anonymity: information travels quickly, and a gender-nonconforming visitor is likely to stand out, with curiosity, staring, awkward misgendering or gossip the most plausible reactions. Health and official services are thin and often require travel to São Filipe or Praia, so everyday friction at lodging or clinics is a likelier concern than any official encounter — and in a small place, a mismatch between documents and presentation is easily noticed and remarked upon. No local law, facility rule, policing pattern or incident directed at trans visitors is documented here, and local attitudes and protections remain uncertain. Recourse runs through national institutions, which function but are distant. The practical exposure is therefore social visibility and service inconvenience rather than legal or organised threat, leaving conditions modestly below the national picture because of small-community scrutiny.

regions.name: Santa Cruz
regions.merged_summary: Santa Cruz is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no concelho-level exception or separate local rule. Santa Cruz is a smaller, semi-rural, close-knit municipality on Santiago that hosts the international airport and part of Praia's urban fringe, and it sees far less international tourism than Praia, Sal or Boa Vista. No region-specific evidence distinguishes Santa Cruz from the national picture: no local legal exception, documented police targeting, organised violence, or protective practice is known for the municipality. Because the available record contains no local data on how trans visitors are treated there, the lack of documented local incidents should not be read as an assurance of safety.

regions.name: São Filipe
regions.merged_summary: São Filipe, the small capital of Fogo island, is subject to Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a traditional, predominantly Catholic town shaped by emigration, with a modest port and far less of a tourist economy than Praia, Sal or Mindelo, so a visibly trans visitor stands out: anonymity is limited and being noticed as a stranger is more likely than in the larger centres. Police, health staff and guesthouse operators here have little training or precedent for handling documents that do not match a visitor's presentation, and the town has no dedicated support or remedy infrastructure — friction over lodging, pharmacies or paperwork tends to be resolved by leaving town or travelling to Praia, with delay. Expect curiosity, staring, misgendering and awkward everyday encounters, and possibly verbal harassment; no São Filipe-specific trans targeting, violence, discriminatory enforcement or organised hostility is documented, and no local protective practice for outed travellers is known. Informal support is thinner than in the capital or the larger resorts, making the everyday picture somewhat less reassuring than the national picture alone suggests — the concern is visibility and thin recourse rather than any documented threat.

regions.name: São Lourenço dos Órgãos
regions.merged_summary:
São Lourenço dos Órgãos is subject to Cabo Verde national law in full, with no local exception.

The municipality is a small, inland, largely rural district of Santiago centred on small towns and rural valleys, with limited international tourism and a smaller institutional footprint than the main tourist islands or Praia. Local services and policing are thin, and no trans-specific support infrastructure is on record. Tight-knit networks and low anonymity mean a visibly trans or document-mismatched visitor is quickly noticed, and community norms here are often described as more conservative than those of the tourist areas. In practice, discovery is more likely to surface as gossip, staring, awkward questioning, or hesitation in hotels, clinics, and local bureaucracy than as organized targeting: there is no documented pattern of local enforcement, sweeps, detention, or violence aimed at transgender visitors in the municipality.

Nothing in the record measures local attitudes toward transgender people specifically, and the wider history of trans-specific violence in the country is limited and undated. Absence of such evidence should not be read as a guarantee of safety — in a small community, exposure tends to be social rather than legal, and practical recourse when something goes wrong is thin. Visitors should weigh the rural, low-anonymity setting alongside the national picture rather than assume either local hostility or a local protective exception.

regions.name: São Miguel
regions.merged_summary:
São Miguel falls squarely under Cabo Verde's national law in full, with no local ordinance on record altering how it applies to trans visitors. Descriptions of the municipality itself vary: it is placed both within the greater Praia urban area and, more often, as a small, agricultural, close-knit interior community on Santiago with a strong Catholic influence and no local trans or LGBT infrastructure. Either way its scale works against anonymity — a visibly trans visitor is conspicuous, and neighbourhood gossip, intrusive questioning or social ostracism are plausible if they are outed. Local observers disagree on whether the municipality sits above or below the national average for tolerance.

The realistic exposures are social and bureaucratic rather than legal: staring, gossip, possible refusal of service, and uncertain assistance from officers.
