Loja is a southern Andean city and province whose capital is a quiet university and regional service centre, with a strongly Catholic and evangelical social character, a large emigrant diaspora and only modest tourism. That setting shapes everyday experience for an openly trans visitor more than any written rule: in a small city anonymity is limited, so being outed, visible discomfort, misgendering, questioning, possible refusal of service and family or neighbourhood pressure are more likely than in larger centres such as Quito or Guayaquil, and families travelling with a gender-nonconforming child may draw added suspicion. Public institutions remain generally accessible, but local sensitivity and enforcement are uneven. No Loja-specific visitor restrictions, trans-targeted enforcement, hostile ordinances or organised or official targeting are documented, and violent-crime pressure is lower than in coastal cities. There is, however, no documented local protection, advocacy infrastructure or inclusive-service record beyond the national baseline, so an outed visitor relies on individual discretion rather than local institutions, and the absence of a recorded pattern of targeted violence should not be read as proof of safety. Local policing and detention feed into the national systems described at country level, so exposure rises sharply if an incident leads to arrest or hospitalisation.

regions.name: Morona Santiago
regions.merged_summary:
Morona Santiago is subject to Ecuador's national law in full, with no local exception.

This is a remote, sparsely populated Amazonian province in the country's southeast, with Macas as its main urban centre and large, dispersed Shuar and Achuar communities. Police, court and prosecutorial presence is thinner outside Macas than in the highland and coastal cities, and hospitals, legal aid and trans-specific support are scarce — so a visitor who is outed is more conspicuous, further from advocacy and complaint channels, and slower to reach help than in Quito or Guayaquil. Everyday expectations are more conservative and church-influenced than in the major urban centres, with customary authority shaping life in indigenous territories and stronger informal social enforcement in small towns; anonymity is limited once outside Macas. Parts of the province have experienced mining-related and armed-group insecurity that raises general risk for anyone travelling there. No province-level protective measures, distinct anti-trans rules, or documented pattern of locally directed targeting are known, so the practical exposure here is stigma, service friction and reduced recourse rather than a separate regional legal penalty.

regions.name: Pichincha
regions.merged_summary: Pichincha is Ecuador's highland province centred on Quito, the capital, and operates within Ecuador's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Quito is the country's most cosmopolitan and tourist-facing city: it has a visible LGBTQ scene, longstanding trans and LGBTI organisations, pride marches, legal-aid and specialist health services, and a metropolitan anti-discrimination ordinance, so everyday encounters are generally more accustomed to gender diversity than in many rural areas. Outside the capital centre, rural Pichincha and the peripheral parishes sit closer to the national picture, and Catholic and machista conservatism persist even in the city, where street-level discrimination, misgendering and service refusal still occur. Police handling of complaints is uneven and the country's security crisis has hardened public life and strained protection here, though the province sees less direct exposure to the armed conflict affecting coastal and border provinces; urban street crime remains relevant. Community support is more accessible in Quito than in most of the country, but it does not amount to an independent protective regime: anyone detained in the capital enters the national custodial system, and the El Encuentro maximum-security facility is in this province. No region-specific evidence establishes routine targeting of trans visitors in Pichincha, nor effective local remedies when they encounter police or custody.

regions.name: Tungurahua
regions.merged_summary: Tungurahua is a small Andean highland province subject to Ecuador's national framework in full, with no local exception or province-specific legislation, protective service or documented anti-trans restriction of its own. What distinguishes it is social texture: Ambato, the capital, is a conservative, heavily Catholic highland commercial city, and the surrounding smaller towns such as Pelileo share that traditional character. A visibly trans visitor there attracts closer scrutiny than in Quito or Guayaquil, with a greater likelihood of intrusive questioning, social hostility or refusal of accommodation, and small-community word-of-mouth reduces anonymity and raises outing exposure. Few LGBT community resources and thin specialist institutional capacity mean encounters with police, clinics, jails or emergency systems carry more friction when help is sought, and seeking police assistance is where local conservatism bites hardest. The canton of Baños de Agua Santa is the contrast: an established international backpacker and tourism hub with a visibly welcoming, visitor-oriented economy and more familiarity with foreign visitors, though it offers no documented local protections of its own. Baños's tolerance does not travel — it fades in the province's smaller communities. No region-specific violence data, facility bans or local visitor-facing practices are documented for Tungurahua, and no local information was found on care access for trans visitors; that gap should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Zamora Chinchipe
regions.merged_summary: Zamora Chinchipe is subject to Ecuador's national regime in full, with no local exception, additional provincial restriction, or documented local protective measure. The province itself is a sparsely populated Amazonian corner of southeastern Ecuador, shaped by small towns such as Zamora, Yantzaza and Gualaquiza, informal mining and border economies, and largely Shuar and Catholic-majority communities. Social conservatism and close-knit conditions mean anonymity is thin: an outed visitor may face persistent scrutiny, gossip, refusal of service or harassment, and services and advocates are concentrated far away in Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca. Police and prosecutorial response is distant and stretched amid national insecurity, so recourse after harassment or denial of care is practically harder to reach here than in the major cities, and no local complaint-handling, trans-aware health care or specialist support infrastructure is documented. Tourism in protected areas brings some foreign visitors, but no local protective infrastructure for them is recorded. No province-specific anti-trans rule, hostile campaign or documented local incident against trans visitors is known, though that reflects limited reporting rather than evidence of safety; equally, the absence of such incidents does not establish it. If a visitor is detained, national custody practices apply, with no documented local protective practice to soften them.

regions.name: Asyut Governorate
regions.merged_summary: Asyut Governorate is subject to Egypt's national regime in full, with no local exception or local safeguard. Asyut sits in Upper Egypt and is markedly more rural, socially and religiously conservative, and less cosmopolitan than Cairo, Alexandria, or the Red Sea resorts. It has little international tourism and few visitor-facing venues, so a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor stands out sharply and cannot rely on the anonymity that tourism economies provide elsewhere in the country. Community-level policing of gender norms is strong, and dense kin and religious networks mean that discovery by neighbours or family acquaintances can trigger social and honour-based hostility independent of any state action. Local queer civil society is barely visible, legal-aid and advocacy resources are concentrated in Cairo, and police and community responses are likely to attract less scrutiny than in the capital. Reporting a problem to local authorities is therefore more likely to worsen a situation than to resolve it, and healthcare or official encounters offer little reliable support. No Asyut-specific campaign against trans visitors and no local protective arrangement has been documented in either direction; that absence reflects a lack of local reporting rather than evidence of safety, and the national exposure applies here without local mitigation.

regions.name: Minya Governate
regions.merged_summary:
Minya is subject to Egypt's national legal regime in full, with no local exception or distinct regional policy known to alter it.

Minya is one of Upper Egypt's most socially conservative governorates: largely rural and agrarian, organised around extended-family and tribal authority, with strong Salafi influence alongside a large Coptic population. It sees far fewer visitors than Cairo or Luxor, and foreign travellers on archaeological itineraries — the sites at Tell el-Amarna and Beni Hasan among them — stand out rather than blend in; there is none of the capital's anonymity, and a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor draws immediate attention. Police checkpoints on Upper Egyptian roads and around those sites involve document checks.

Support infrastructure that exists in the capital is absent here: no trans organisation, legal clinic or advocacy group operates in Minya, and the country's principal advocacy and legal-aid bodies work from Cairo. Local conditions compound rather than soften the national picture. Discovery is more likely to travel through community channels — neighbours, family, informal religious authority — than through official ones, bringing honour-based pressure and informal violence with little realistic recourse. Police handling and public services follow local norms, with weaker institutional restraint and almost no prospect of an advocate intervening, and complaints can carry their own risk. No documented local protective exception, regional exemption or effective local remedy is known.

regions.name: Qena Governorate
regions.merged_summary:
Qena Governorate is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception.

Qena lies in Upper Egypt and is largely rural and small-city, well away from Cairo's advocacy, consular and legal-aid infrastructure. Society here is socially conservative, with strong clan, family and religious authority policing gender norms, few foreign residents, and little visible LGBT or trans community organisation. The Nile temple corridor around Dendera brings some visitor-facing familiarity with foreigners, but it offers no cover away from the sites, and there is no documented local protective measure, shelter practice, or sign of lighter police treatment than the national pattern.

In practice, a trans visitor who is recognised or outed in Qena has fewer buffers than in Cairo or the Red Sea resorts: less anonymity in crowds and expatriate life, thinner informal support, and greater dependence on communities where news travels through tight networks. Local material records no governorate-specific incidents involving trans travellers, so the picture here rests on these social conditions rather than on documented Qena cases, and that absence should not be read as softening the national picture. Recourse after an arrest or extortion attempt is likely to be slower and more distant than in the capital, and no local sources describe separate outcomes for a travelling minor or guardian.

regions.name: Red Sea Governorate
regions.merged_summary: Red Sea Governorate is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. Its coast — Hurghada, El Gouna, Safaga, Quseir and Marsa Alam — is the country's main resort corridor, built on foreign tourism, with large resort compounds, private security, a substantial expatriate and visitor presence, and tourism police along the shoreline; alcohol is widely served in the resort enclaves and foreign visitors are routine. Street-level scrutiny of foreigners is lighter than in metropolitan centres or rural Upper Egypt, so everyday interactions and public presentation can be more relaxed, and hotel staff may exercise pragmatic discretion. That shielding is informal: hotel registration, ID checks and the national security apparatus apply throughout the governorate, and a document check or complaint in a coastal town can still escalate as it would elsewhere in Egypt. The desert interior and Bedouin areas are more socially conservative and offer no additional protection, and remote locations can intensify vulnerability rather than lessen it. No pattern of trans-targeted enforcement specific to this governorate, and no local protective practice or documented enforcement divergence, is on record; that absence should not be read as safety, and local social responses and the treatment of travelling minors remain uncertain.

regions.name: Sohag Governorate
regions.merged_summary:
Sohag Governorate is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception.

Sohag is a largely rural governorate in deep Upper Egypt, far less cosmopolitan than Cairo, Alexandria or the Red Sea resorts, with stronger clan, family and religious authority and small close-knit communities where a visibly gender-nonconforming outsider attracts intense attention. Foreign visitors come mainly for the Abydos archaeology sites and the Coptic monasteries; tourist-facing accommodation, hotels and English-language advocacy channels are thin, and there is little anonymous urban space in which to go unnoticed. The governorate has no queer community infrastructure and no tolerant nightlife sphere, and it has far less NGO monitoring, legal aid and press scrutiny than the capital — so discovery would likely travel quickly through community and family networks where honour and religious norms are strongly enforced, and any recourse after detention, eviction or assault is farther away and harder to reach.

Local police operate with less oversight and fewer foreign witnesses than in the capital, and nothing in Sohag's record documents local exceptions, protective practices or remedies working in a trans visitor's favour. No Sohag-specific incident involving a trans visitor is established in the available material; that thinness reflects limited documentation and uncertainty rather than evidence of safer conditions, and social hostility here runs deeper than the national picture.

regions.name: South Sinai Governorate
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Egypt's national law in full, with no local exception. South Sinai's character is set by the Red Sea resort corridor of Sharm el-Sheikh, Dahab and Nuweiba, where an internationally oriented hospitality sector, English-speaking tourist services and constant exposure to foreign guests mean gender-nonconforming presentation is often read simply as foreign; in Dahab especially, dive and backpacker communities maintain an informal tolerance, and open hostility toward tourists is uncommon. Against that, the governorate is heavily securitised: military and police checkpoints line coastal roads and sit at airports, ferry terminals and border crossings with routine identity checks, hotels register guest documents with security forces, and the Bedouin interior and non-tourist towns remain socially conservative, with no local legal aid or protective institutions. Local security attention concentrates on border and resort policing rather than routine morality sweeps against visitors — an emphasis, not a safeguard. Day-to-day friction in the resort enclaves is therefore lower than in most of Egypt, but the softening is social rather than legal: discovery at a checkpoint, in hotel registration, or in any police encounter returns a visitor to the same national machinery as elsewhere, with nothing local to cushion it. Outside the resort strip conditions are less documented and should be treated as more uncertain.

regions.name: Anseba Region
regions.merged_summary: The Anseba Region is subject to Eritrea's national regime in full, with no local exception. Anseba is a largely rural highland area centred on Keren, where social and religious community life is close-knit. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture in enforcement, protections, or day-to-day conditions for a trans visitor, and no local incidents, protective mechanisms, or remedies are documented here. That absence of local reporting should not be read as reassurance: visitors should assume the conditions recorded at country level apply in Anseba as well.

regions.name: Debub Region
regions.merged_summary: Debub Region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. Debub is a largely rural highland province centred on Mendefera, with strong Orthodox and Muslim community norms, fewer foreign residents and visitors, fewer visitor facilities than the capital, and sparser medical and legal services. Internal travel permits and checkpoints are routine across this heavily militarised interior, so a trans visitor's identity may come up at transit points, ID checks or accommodation registration; anonymity is lower than in Asmara and small-town community scrutiny is tighter. Local officials and security personnel operate with little practical accountability, and a mismatch in documents or presentation can be escalated by an individual into detention, deportation, extortion or referral to punitive custody. No local protection, tolerance signal or LGBTQ community infrastructure is documented anywhere in the region, and there is no independent recourse if things go wrong. The lack of local records on how the regime is applied here should not be read as safety: state censorship limits what becomes documented, and moral-policing pressure in these communities may be stronger than in the capital.

regions.name: Gash-Barka Region
regions.merged_summary:
Gash-Barka is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception.

The region is Eritrea's rural western lowland agricultural heartland, bordering Sudan and Ethiopia, made up of small towns and tight community networks where anonymity is hard to come by. Few foreign residents live here, tourism and service infrastructure is minimal, and the distance from Asmara's diplomatic, legal and community resources means consular or advocacy help is unlikely to arrive quickly. Strong traditional and religious norms are matched by a visible security presence: checkpoints and internal movement permits make document and appearance checks routine, so a trans visitor is scrutinised more often, and in less forgiving settings, than in the capital. Incidents go unreported locally; the region's silence on such matters reflects a thin, censored record rather than evidence of tolerance or safety. Discovery is therefore more likely to be settled through customary disapproval and state coercion, with little local recourse, few informal safe spaces, and no credible protection nearby.

regions.name: Maekel Region
regions.merged_summary:
Maekel Region lies wholly under Eritrea's national regime, with no local exception.

The region is dominated by Asmara, the capital and administrative centre, where the country's police, courts, prisons, immigration apparatus and foreign missions are concentrated and where checkpoints, document checks and scrutiny of foreign residents are densest. Every enforcement action in Eritrea's documented record — arrests of men suspected of same-sex conduct and the expulsion of foreign workers and a foreign teacher — took place in Asmara itself, making Maekel the enforcement geography of the country rather than a gentler periphery; those incidents are dated, no more recent local case or trans-specific enforcement is documented, and so they show where enforcement happens rather than how often it occurs. Asmara's urban, comparatively cosmopolitan character, its tourism profile and its large foreign and diplomatic presence offer no documented local shield: street anonymity and proximity to embassies do not extend to official encounters, and the visibility of foreigners appears to raise scrutiny rather than reduce it. Public spaces are conservative and closely watched, and there is no local record of protective policing, sanctuary practice, community organisations or any other infrastructure offering trans visitors support or remedy. A trans traveller who is outed here is likely to face police questioning, confinement in facilities with a documented record of abuse, and expulsion or prosecution, with little practical recourse.

regions.name: Northen Red Sea Region
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Eritrea's national law in full, with no local exception. The Northern Red Sea Region centres on the port of Massawa and the Dahlak ferry routes, a coastal strip with a visible security presence and routine identity and document checks. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this area from the national picture: nothing documents local tolerance, protective enforcement, community support or complaint mechanisms for trans visitors in Massawa, Assab, the Dahlak coast or the inland districts, and no local exception to national law or enforcement is known — nor should that absence of local reporting be read as reassurance. A visitor should expect the conditions described for Eritrea to apply here, with checkpoint scrutiny meaning that an identity-document mismatch can itself draw further questioning.

regions.name: Southern Red Sea Region
regions.merged_summary: The Southern Red Sea Region is subject to Eritrea's national regime in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture for a transgender visitor. As setting rather than legal variation, it is a remote, sparsely populated lowland port area centred on Assab, distant from the capital, with thin civilian services, limited medical and legal infrastructure, and a visible security presence along the coast and borders — conditions that leave a visitor with little practical access to lawyers or consular help should something go wrong. The lack of documented local differences should not be read as reassurance: nothing indicates conditions milder than the national ones, and no local tolerance, protective practice or lighter enforcement is known.

regions.name: Ida-Viru maakond
regions.merged_summary: Ida-Viru maakond is subject to Estonia's national legal framework in full, with no local exception, and no county bylaw, pattern of police targeting or trans-specific violence record distinguishing it from the national picture has been documented. Local differences are social rather than legal: the county — Narva, Kohtla-Järve and Sillamäe — is Estonia's most heavily Russian-speaking and post-industrial region, with more conservative public attitudes toward gender and sexuality than Tallinn, and Russian-language media carrying more weight. An outed trans visitor should expect staring, misgendering, intrusive curiosity and awkward document or service checks, with Russian-language venues generally less familiar with trans identities; these frictions are likeliest in smaller towns and rural areas, and anonymity is thinner than in the capital. LGBT community infrastructure, specialist support and trans-led organisations are concentrated in Tallinn, so language support and help-seeking are less convenient here, and continuity of gender-related care or affirming local practice is not documented. National police, courts and equality institutions retain jurisdiction in the county, though county-level experience handling trans visitors' cases is not documented — the practical concern is social friction and stigma rather than documented official hostility.

regions.name: Hareri
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Ethiopia's national law in full, with no local exception. Harari centres on the walled city of Harar in eastern Ethiopia — a small, tightly knit, overwhelmingly Muslim and socially conservative city-region whose historic old town is a tourist destination and whose strong guest-hospitality tradition softens everyday encounters with visitors. Against that, a foreigner here is conspicuous: the region's small scale, tight community networks and tourism-facing old town leave little anonymity, so families and neighbours effectively act as informal enforcers, and discovery of a trans visitor's status can bring ostracism and community pressure beyond what the national picture alone implies. No region-specific enforcement record, lighter local application, or protective mechanism was identified for Harari, and regional religious and community norms appear to deepen concealment pressures rather than relieve them; if an outing occurs, recourse remains thin and police protection weak. Equally, the absence of Harari-specific incidents should not be read as safety — no local mitigation offsets the national pattern for a trans traveller.

regions.name: Central Finland
regions.merged_summary: Central Finland is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. Regionally, life is centred on Jyväskylä, a university city with a visible student and LGBTQ community and mainstream healthcare, hospitality and transport infrastructure; tourism and the academic presence reduce the isolation felt elsewhere inland. Outside the city, smaller municipalities are more socially conservative and less anonymous, so a visibly trans visitor is more likely to meet staring, misgendering, awkward questioning or open disapproval than in the capital — everyday friction rather than organised hostility. No local pattern of police targeting, facility bans, border or document practice, or custody rules aimed at trans visitors is known in the region, and public services generally accept identity documents as issued. The practical weak points for a visitor are bureaucratic or care-access friction and occasional public harassment, with ordinary recourse available; specialist trans-affirming care is not offered locally, so anyone who may need it during the visit should arrange it beforehand.

regions.name: Finland Proper
regions.merged_summary: Finland Proper is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is anchored by Turku, a university, port and ferry city with an established Pride tradition, a visible organised LGBT community, an English-friendly environment and concentrated public services including emergency care; everyday interaction in the city tends to be respectful, and public services, hospitality and transport operate without trans-specific exclusion. There are no local ordinances restricting facility access and no documented pattern of official targeting, document scrutiny or police hostility toward trans visitors in the region; reported harassment is handled through ordinary police channels, and recourse depends on making a report. Outside Turku, the smaller municipalities of Varsinais-Suomi are more socially conservative and trans visibility is lower, so friction, staring or misgendering is more likely there than in the regional centre, though no documented pattern of denial of entry or exclusion from facilities exists. For a visitor whose trans status becomes known, the realistic exposure in this region is everyday social friction or occasional verbal harassment with working recourse, rather than organised violence or official sanction.

regions.name: Kainuu
regions.merged_summary:
Kainuu is a sparsely populated rural region in northeastern Finland, and it is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. No regional statute, facility rule, or documented trans-specific incident has been identified in the area.

Kainuu's character shapes everyday experience more than its legal framework. The region is thinly populated and small-town, with few anonymous urban spaces, so an outed visitor may find that curiosity, staring, misgendering, awkward questions, or conservative disapproval surface more easily than they would in a large city — though this reflects social texture rather than organized hostility or official hostility. Ordinary friction, if any, is more likely to appear in accommodation, healthcare, or public venues than in encounters with the authorities. Anonymity is lower in small communities, and there is limited local trans-specific health or support services; gender-affirming care is concentrated in a few larger Finnish cities, so a visitor needing such care in Kainuu would face travel and waiting-time delays rather than refusal. The smaller queer community presence and lower everyday visibility of the region relative to the metropolitan south can also mean more isolation for a trans traveller.

Tourism centres such as Kajaani and Vuokatti encounter outside visitors routinely, and schools and services across the region operate under the same inclusive national rules as elsewhere in Finland. There is no documented pattern of police mistreatment, violence, or organized anti-trans campaigning in Kainuu, and no known local ordinances targeting trans people; the practical concerns here are visibility and service geography rather than legal danger.

regions.name: Kymenlaakso
regions.merged_summary: Kymenlaakso is subject to Finland's national legal framework in full, with no local exception or additional restriction. The region is a small, relatively traditional south-eastern corner of the country centred on the towns of Kouvola and Kotka near the Russian border, where a visibly trans visitor may stand out more than in the capital and could encounter curiosity or mild awkwardness in everyday encounters. Beyond that, no region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Kymenlaakso from the national picture: nothing documented indicates local variation in policing, border or facility handling, healthcare access for visitors, or official response to trans people.

regions.name: Northern Savonia
regions.merged_summary: Northern Savonia is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture for a transgender visitor. The region is largely rural and centred on Kuopio, a university and hospital town with a steady flow of visitors; smaller towns and rural municipalities may be less accustomed to trans people, so staring, misgendering, awkward service interactions or bureaucratic curiosity are more plausible there than in larger Finnish cities. What is documented nationally — anti-LGBT incidents and delays in obtaining gender-related care — indicates possible social or service friction rather than a demonstrated rate of harm to visitors, and a visitor needing care, including a minor travelling with a guardian, may meet waiting times under national clinical guidance rather than a refusal. Border targeting, facility exclusion, custody practices and local violence rates are not documented here, and such silence should not be read as evidence that these risks are absent.

regions.name: Pirkanmaa
regions.merged_summary: Pirkanmaa is subject to Finnish national law in full, with no local exception. The region is anchored by Tampere, a large university and service city with a visibly active LGBT community, annual Pride events, university-linked LGBTIQ organisations and Seta-affiliated services, alongside municipal equality work. Tampere University Hospital hosts one of the country's two centralised gender identity units, so gender-affirming care is accessed locally rather than requiring travel elsewhere in Finland. Public services, transport and accommodation in Tampere generally operate without identity-based exclusion, and no region-specific enforcement practice, facility restriction, or organised hostility toward trans visitors is documented. The surrounding rural municipalities of Pirkanmaa are more socially conservative than the Tampere urban core, but this shows up as ordinary social friction — misgendering, staring or occasional individual service friction from particular providers or communities — rather than as regional policy; adverse treatment there is shaped by individual attitudes rather than any local rule. National reporting on rising suspected hate-crime incidents involving sexual orientation or gender identity applies to the region in general, but no Pirkanmaa-specific rate or visitor-facing risk is established. For travelling families, the fact that gender identity care is concentrated in the Tampere unit can mean waiting times if care is sought during a stay, though this is not a restriction on visiting with a trans minor. Overall, conditions in the region track the national picture closely: the urban core is comparatively open and familiar to trans visitors, while conservative areas offer social rather than legal friction.

regions.name: Päijät-Häme
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. Päijät-Häme is a southern region centred on Lahti, about an hour from Helsinki, where the city provides the main accommodation, transport, policing and venues, while surrounding municipalities such as Heinola, Hollola and Orimattila are smaller and more traditional — thinner trans community infrastructure and less consistent staff awareness make everyday friction, staring or awkward encounters more likely here than in the capital. No local legal departure, policing pattern or documented hostility toward trans visitors distinguishes Päijät-Häme from the national picture, and that lack of locally distinguishing reports should not be read as a guarantee of safety for an individual visit.

regions.name: South Karelia
regions.merged_summary: South Karelia is Finland's south-eastern border region, centred on Lappeenranta and Imatra. The region is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. It is more rural and older, and socially more conventional, than Helsinki or the university cities: smaller towns and tight-knit communities mean less anonymity and greater visibility for a trans visitor, and LGBTQ venues and specialist services are correspondingly scarce. Public attitudes here are less internationally exposed than in the capital, which can translate into staring, curiosity, misgendering, occasional unfamiliarity with mismatched documents or care pathways, and general service friction rather than threat. Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided within the region, so a visitor needing continuity of treatment should expect travel and waiting time; everyday settings such as emergency care, hotels and transport are routine, and police and courts are functioning institutions that take complaints. No region-specific trans-related statute, enforcement pattern, documented incident of anti-trans violence, police targeting or facility exclusion is known here — the practical exposure is social rather than official. The region sits on the Schengen external border with Russia, where crossings are governed by Finnish rules and ordinary document scrutiny can be somewhat more frequent than elsewhere in the country, including for travellers whose passport marker or name differs from their presentation. No trans-specific check is a known local practice, and cross-border traffic adds no documented trans-specific exposure.

regions.name: Southern Savonia
regions.merged_summary: Southern Savonia is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception, and no distinct regional trans-specific rule, enforcement practice or official hostility is known. The region is a rural, sparsely populated lake district in eastern Finland centred on Mikkeli and Savonlinna, with an older and more socially traditional population than Helsinki and fewer LGBT organisations and services than the capital. Local social reactions and service experiences remain uncertain, but the likely everyday outcome of being recognised as trans in small towns and villages is curiosity, awkward misgendering or mild service friction rather than organised targeting; there is no documented local pattern of anti-trans violence, official abuse or ordinance-based restriction. Practical differences from the metropolitan picture are mostly about access: specialist gender care and peer networks are centralised elsewhere, local health and administrative staff may have narrower experience with gender-diverse people, and a visitor needing routine or emergency care could encounter unfamiliarity or delay. Institutions still function — police and courts operate under national obligations and record hate-crime motive data, and no local institutional barrier to trans visitors is identified — though reported national hate-crime suspicion figures do not establish prevalence here. Anonymity is thinner than in a large city, so discretion about being outed rests more on small-community familiarity than on any legal exposure. Seasonal tourism around Savonlinna's opera period, along with lake cruises, hotels and public venues, is accustomed to visitors and operates under the same national equality framework as the rest of the country.

regions.name: Tavastia Proper
regions.merged_summary: Tavastia Proper is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. The region covers southern inland Finland around Hämeenlinna, Riihimäki, Forssa and Lahti, with substantial rural countryside between them; no local ordinance, policing practice, facility restriction or documented incident targets transgender visitors. In practice the main local difference from the capital is social rather than legal: these are smaller, less diverse towns where a visibly trans traveller may draw staring, curiosity, awkward misgendering or intrusive questions in everyday services, and somewhat more so in nightlife and accommodation settings, though this remains friction rather than official hostility. Local trans-specific resources are thin, and specialist gender-care is centralised, with the nearest gender identity units in Tampere and Helsinki, so routine and emergency services are accessible but specialised care is not locally prominent. Practical exposure centres on routine document checks and the discretion of small businesses rather than any credible legal or custodial threat; police and health staff operate under nationally applied training and ordinary Finnish administrative practice, and no local pattern of targeting, extortion or exclusion of trans visitors is recorded.

regions.name: Uusimaa
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Finland's national law in full, with no local exception. Uusimaa, containing Helsinki, Espoo and Vantaa, is Finland's most urban, internationally diverse and socially liberal region, with the country's strongest LGBT community infrastructure: large public Pride events with official participation, openly trans residents and venues, and the centralised gender identity clinics that deliver the country's gender-affirming care. Its tourism-facing services — Helsinki-Vantaa border control, hotels, transit and clinics — routinely handle foreign documents, including mismatched gender markers, as an ordinary matter, and no pattern of trans-specific screening or official targeting of visitors is documented there. Police in the metropolitan area are accustomed to diverse presentations and treat reports as routine, with incidents met by investigation and prosecution rather than impunity. Because most recorded hate-motivated offences in the country concentrate in the metropolitan area, street-level harassment and occasional service friction remain a real but generally low-severity exposure. The likelier inconvenience for a visitor is administrative: passport or presentation questions at airports, hotels or medical appointments, or waiting times when seeking continuity of gender-affirming care, which bear more heavily on residents than on short-stay visitors. Everyday outing tends to carry less consequence here than elsewhere in Finland, though mild curiosity and bureaucratic questions about documents can still occur.

regions.name: Åland Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Åland Islands are subject to Finnish national law in full, with no local exception.

Åland is an autonomous, demilitarised, Swedish-speaking archipelago of roughly 30,000 people, with Mariehamn as its tourist centre and a tourism-dependent economy accustomed to foreign visitors. Health and education are administered by Åland's own authorities rather than mainland bodies, so specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally: anyone needing it is referred to mainland Finland, with the waiting times that entails. Practically, the more significant local difference is scale. It is a small, close-knit island society where anonymity is thin and word travels quickly, and where a visibly trans foreigner is more conspicuous than in Helsinki. Rural social attitudes tend to be somewhat more conventional than in the capital, and tight-community visibility raises the likelihood of staring, awkward misgendering, gossip, or local officials knowing one another — socially uncomfortable, but no documented pattern of hostility or violence follows from it.

No Åland-specific criminal provision, document rule, facility restriction, or enforcement practice affecting trans visitors is documented, and no trans-specific incidents or police targeting are recorded for the islands. However, region-specific knowledge of local enforcement is limited, and the absence of documented incidents is not itself evidence of safety: border, custody, facility and emergency-care practices are simply not recorded at Åland level. Finnish remedies, courts and emergency care remain available, and the tolerant Nordic street-level climate that visitors encounter appears to reflect general social norms rather than any distinct protective regime.

regions.name: Central
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Fiji's national law in full, with no local exception. Central Division is anchored by Suva, the capital and largest city and the seat of government and most police, court and hospital institutions, so formal encounters where paperwork or presentation is checked are more common here than in outer divisions, and complaint routes are more accessible than in remote areas. Suva is also Fiji's most urban and internationally connected centre: it hosts the country's principal vaka sa lewa lewa community, visible LGBT organising and Pride activity, advocacy and health organisations, and university and government settings where gender-nonconforming presentation is comparatively familiar, with a diverse hospitality sector offering more anonymity for visitors. Against this, conservative church influence remains strong across the division's towns and peri-urban areas, and public life outside central neighbourhoods is less forgiving. Distrust of police in Suva itself is documented, so reporting harm is discouraged and recourse for a trans visitor is thin and uneven. Suva is also where a young transgender woman was killed in 2018; that case is serious but does not establish a rate or pattern. No Central-specific criminalisation, facility ban, border practice or additional protection distinguishing the division from national law is known.

regions.name: Western
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Fiji's national law in full, with no local exception. Western Fiji is the country's principal tourism and transport corridor, centred on Nadi International Airport, the Denarau resort zone, Lautoka, the sugar belt and the Mamanuca, Yasawa and Coral Coast resorts; hotels, tour operators and police here handle foreign guests and their documents daily, and no local statute, facility rule or documented enforcement practice restricts transgender visitors. As the main international gateway, Nadi is the one point where a mismatch between a traveller's presentation and their home passport could prompt border questioning, though no systematic targeting of trans travellers is documented. Because Fiji has no gender-marker change process, a visitor's home-issued documents govern throughout. Social conditions vary within the division: resort and town settings are comparatively accustomed to diversity and routine contact with foreign visitors, while Lautoka, Ba and the sugar-belt communities — with their Methodist, Catholic, Hindu and Muslim congregations — and rural areas such as Rakiraki and the interior remain more socially conservative, where visible non-conformity is likelier to draw comment. Outside tourist zones, service friction is plausible and recourse after harassment is uncertain; no Western-specific criminalisation, detention pattern or documented violence against trans travellers is identified, and the documented 2018 killing of a trans woman occurred in Suva, outside this division.

regions.name: Centre-Val de Loire
regions.merged_summary: Centre-Val de Loire is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception, and no region-specific legislation, protection or restriction governing transgender visitors has been identified here. What distinguishes the region is its scale and social texture: a largely rural area of mid-sized, socially centre-right cities — Orléans, Tours, Blois, Chartres and Bourges — set among the château country of the Loire Valley, markedly less cosmopolitan than Paris and Île-de-France. Day-to-day exposure in small towns and the countryside tends to be ordinary staring-level curiosity rather than organised hostility, and the tourist-facing hospitality of the Loire Valley modestly softens that friction. Trans community infrastructure and trans-affirming clinicians are thin outside Tours, so a visitor needing specialist services, correct name or gender handling, or institutional support may find fewer options than in the capital; provincial settings can also mean more visible misgendering and administrative scrutiny, with anonymity harder to come by than in a large city. Police, courts and oversight bodies operate on the national system, and no local police sweeps, border practices or facility-specific rules differing from the national pattern are documented. Practical exposure therefore runs close to the countrywide picture, shaped mainly by a quieter, less anonymous and less well-served environment.

regions.name: Grand Est
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to French national law in full, with no local exception. Grand Est adds no trans-specific restrictions of its own, and what shapes a trans visitor's experience here is geography and social texture rather than any local rule. Strasbourg hosts the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights alongside a substantial urban LGBT infrastructure — associations, Pride events and daily cross-border life with Germany — which makes official and service-provider encounters there comparatively routine. Metz, Nancy and Reims are similarly larger, university cities with visible LGBTQ communities, and the region's visitor economy (the Alsace Christmas markets, Colmar, Reims) is habituated to an international, mixed clientele. Away from those centres, the rural Vosges, Ardennes and parts of Champagne and Alsace are more socially conservative, with a thinner LGBTQ presence; Alsace-Moselle also retains its own local legal tradition within a practising Catholic milieu. Strasbourg's international character partly offsets that conservatism, leaving the difference from the national picture one of degree rather than kind. Because the region sits on Schengen borders — crossings into Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and Switzerland, including Mulhouse–Basel — identity documents may be checked more often here than inland, and periodic security and immigration controls add to that routine scrutiny. No organised targeting specific to the region is documented.

regions.name: Chuuk
regions.merged_summary: Chuuk is subject to Micronesia (FSM) national law in full, with no local exception. Locally, it is one of the more socially conservative states: a predominantly Christian, church-centred society with strong traditional family norms, where gender variance is likely to be less accepted than the national picture suggests. Chuuk's small, tightly-knit island communities leave little anonymity — tourism is limited, so a visibly transgender visitor may stand out and attract curiosity, disapproval, and family or community scrutiny, particularly for a traveller accompanied by a minor. Institutional support is thin: police and court capacity is limited outside Weno, and formal complaint recourse on the outer islands is minimal, so everyday social friction has no meaningful local remedy. No documented pattern of trans-specific police targeting, custody abuse, facility restrictions, or organized violence in Chuuk is known, but this absence of local incident records should not be read as evidence of safety. The principal local exposure is social stigma and visibility rather than documented legal enforcement, and no region-specific protection or visitor remedy has been shown to operate here.

regions.name: Pohnpei
regions.merged_summary:
Pohnpei is subject to Micronesia (FSM) national law in full, with no local exception.

As the federation's capital island, Pohnpei holds the national capital Palikir, the state government, the College of Micronesia, Kolonia's international airport and the country's largest expatriate, diplomatic and agency presence. It is the most urbanised, populous and tourist-facing of the four states, with hotels, a hospital and widely spoken English, and foreign visitors — including those with unconventional gender presentation — are a routine rather than sensational presence; police and service encounters tend to be low-key, and foreign documents are processed without gender-specific challenge.

The same social currents that shape the country as a whole are felt locally through strong Christian church influence, traditional chiefly authority and small, close-knit communities in which a visitor is quickly noticed. The likely outcomes of being noticed are social rather than legal: misgendering, staring, gossip and some service friction. No trans-targeted policing, facility exclusion or violence is documented locally, and no pattern of official hostility toward trans visitors is known; on the other hand, the police and courts are small-scale and offer little proactive recourse, and trans-specific services are effectively absent, so a visitor who encounters difficulty would rely mainly on informal tolerance and hospitality. Everyday conservatism here reads more as social friction than documented hostility, and nothing in Pohnpei's local conditions materially worsens the national picture.

regions.name: Yap
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Micronesia (FSM) national law in full, with no local exception. Yap is a small, traditionally governed island state of roughly eleven thousand people, with a chiefly and caste-based hierarchy and strong Catholic and Protestant church influence shaping conservative gender roles. A visibly gender-nonconforming foreign visitor is conspicuous: tightly connected village and lodgings settings, families and hosts, and fast-moving gossip mean anonymity is essentially unavailable, and a mismatched marker or nonconforming presentation can become widely known quickly. The realistic exposure is social rather than institutional — curiosity, staring, misgendering, gossip, community scrutiny, informal pressure and possible awkwardness with services — rather than arrest. There is no documented record in Yap of police or judicial targeting of transgender travellers, service refusal on those grounds, or anti-trans violence; police and courts operate under the national framework and US-compact arrangements. That silence should not be read as proof of safety: local evidence is thin, and reporting on societal stigma nationally is dated and lacks trans-specific detail, so current consequences of visibility remain uncertain. Practical support is limited — health care, lodging and facilities are sparse, with no trans-specific services or advocacy infrastructure on the island — so visitors should plan for self-reliance, carry their own supplies, and expect that any friction encountered will be handled informally through community norms rather than through a formal complaint route.

regions.name: Estuaire
regions.merged_summary: Estuaire falls under Gabon's national regime in full, with no local legal exception. The province is the country's most urban and most foreign-facing, centred on Libreville and its international airport and seaport — the busiest arrival and screening points in Gabon — with surrounding urban, diplomatic, hotel and business corridors. That scale, along with a large expatriate and diplomatic population, a lively nightlife and a cosmopolitan mix, gives a trans visitor more anonymity and informal tolerance than smaller centres offer, and some services exist if a complaint has to be made. Against this, Libreville's routine police checkpoints and document checks raise the chance that a mismatch between presentation and identity documents comes to official attention; if that happens, friction, invasive questioning, refusal of service or detention-based embarrassment remain possible, and recourse for a harassed visitor tends to be informal and uncertain. Facilities, custody and care follow birth sex, with no documented local remedy. Social conservatism can still produce harassment by individuals, described as common, and bureaucratic delay, and no documented local protection, ordinance or pattern of distinct hostility toward trans visitors is known. The lack of reported Estuaire cases should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Haut-Ogooué
regions.merged_summary: Haut-Ogooué is subject to Gabon's national law in full, with no local exception. The province centres on Franceville and the Moanda mining towns, where a mining economy brings foreign residents and expatriate communities, but where smaller communities and tight social visibility make a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor far more conspicuous than in Libreville. Customary and religious authority is strong in the provincial towns, anonymity is limited, and staring, questioning, refusal of services or an arbitrary police stop are realistic consequences of being read as gender-nonconforming. The province is also the Bongo family's home region, giving it a political profile distinct from the rest of the country. There is no local LGBTQ+ organisation, dedicated legal aid or advocacy network to turn to, and consular or NGO assistance is distant; remedies that exist in principle are weaker outside the capital. Remote border crossings involve more discretionary document checks, adding friction conditional on discovery, with consequences tending toward questioning, demands for bribes and humiliation in dealings with services rather than custody campaigns. No region-specific record documents police targeting, arrests or violence against transgender visitors here, so the province's added exposure comes from visibility, social conservatism and isolation rather than distinct local law. The absence of local evidence should not be read as a sign of safety.

regions.name: Moyen-Ogooué
regions.merged_summary:
Moyen-Ogooué is subject to Gabon's national law in full, with no local exception.

This is an interior, largely rural province centred on Lambaréné, a small river town on the Ogooué with a hospital, a port and logging traffic, and little of the anonymity available in Libreville or Port-Gentil; it has no significant tourist economy. A visibly transgender visitor stands out here — word travels quickly, and hotels, clinics and police contact are common points at which a mismatched passport or non-conforming presentation can lead to being outed. Police, medical and hospitality staff are fewer and less trained than on the coast, so everyday encounters involve uneven official discretion, staring, invasive questioning and refusals, while formal remedies largely depend on Libreville. Local social settings are comparatively conservative, and the province offers thinner institutional, service and community support than the capital, with no documented local safeguarding or mitigation.

No province-specific campaign, hostile enforcement pattern or documented local violence against trans visitors is known — but this reflects limited local documentation rather than confirmed safety, and the absence of recorded incidents should not be read as absence of risk.

regions.name: Ngounié
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Gabon's national law in full, with no local exception. Ngounié is a largely rural inland province centred on the town of Mouila, with small, closely connected settlements, socially conservative public life and limited tourist infrastructure. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this province from the national picture: no local laws, incidents or official practices affecting trans visitors, and no local exception either protective or hostile, are documented. The lack of such local evidence should not be read as an indication of safety, and the absence of province-specific documentation means visitors should not assume either tolerance or hostility in advance.

regions.name: Nyanga
regions.merged_summary: Nyanga is subject to Gabon's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a sparsely populated, forested southern Atlantic area centred on Tchibanga, with far thinner tourist, medical and legal-aid infrastructure than Libreville, low anonymity in small towns and limited options for departure. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Nyanga from the national picture for a trans visitor: no local law, enforcement pattern, court practice or protective mechanism specific to the province appears in the record. The absence of a documented local incident should not be read as safety — how an outed visitor would be treated and what recourse would actually be effective in the province remain uncertain.

regions.name: Ogooué-Ivindo
regions.merged_summary: Ogooué-Ivindo is subject to Gabon's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. The province is a sparsely populated, heavily forested northeastern area centred on Makokou, with small, tightly knit communities. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this region from the national picture. Local enforcement practices, prevailing social attitudes, and the availability of trained officials or effective recourse in the province remain uncertain rather than documented, and nothing in this summary should be taken as evidence of local research. Because absence of local reports is not evidence of safety, a trans visitor should treat the practical conditions here as unverified: what applies on paper nationally may be harder to reach in practice in a remote inland province, and any difficulty encountered locally would likely be shaped by informal rather than formal channels.

regions.name: Ogooué-Lolo
regions.merged_summary: Ogooué-Lolo is subject to Gabon's national law in full, with no local exception. The province is a remote, sparsely populated interior region of forest and rural communities, centred on its capital Koulamoutou, with administrative and logging towns along the railway, little tourist traffic and no trans-specific community or advocacy infrastructure. In small, tight-knit provincial towns a visibly trans foreigner attracts sustained attention and word travels quickly through employers, guesthouses and clinics, so anonymity that might be available elsewhere is hard to keep; strong rural social conservatism adds to community scrutiny. Institutional presence is thin: police and judicial infrastructure is weaker than in the capital, oversight of local officials is limited, and there are fewer discreet services, alternative support organisations or complaint mechanisms, so an outed visitor has less practical recourse than in Libreville. The nearest specialist services, legal assistance and consular access are in Libreville or Franceville. Health and lodging staff have little familiarity with foreign documents or transition-related care, making disclosure at clinics and hotels more likely and harder to manage. No province-specific pattern of targeted police action, violence or effective protective service is documented here, but that absence should not be read as proof of safety.

regions.name: Ogooué-Maritime
regions.merged_summary:
Ogooué-Maritime is subject to Gabon's national legal framework in full, with no local exception.

The province's character is set by Port-Gentil, the country's oil and port hub: an urban, transactional, internationally staffed city where outsider status is routine and a substantial expatriate community gives a trans visitor more anonymity and contact with foreign workers than rural provinces. The coastal tourism belt around Loango, Mayumba and Pongara also receives foreign visitors regularly, and no record of local authorities targeting gender-nonconforming travellers is known. Away from these settings — the province's fishing villages, small towns and remote park areas — small-community scrutiny is tighter, being outed carries more consequence, and access to advocacy or legal support is limited. Social conservatism and misgendering friction remain plausible outside expatriate and tourist circles, and social hostility toward visible non-conformity is real.

Anonymity at the port does not extend to formal encounters: document or presentation mismatches can surface at airport and port entry, hotel checks and police stops, where weak oversight and the absence of a reliable complaint mechanism leave informal payments as a recurring risk. No Ogooué-Maritime-specific trans protections, organised anti-trans campaign, targeting pattern or custody pathway is known to distinguish the region from the national picture, and the province's cosmopolitan port character offers modest everyday buffering rather than any substantive local safeguard. Thin regional evidence resolves close to the national picture, with somewhat less urban cover outside Port-Gentil.

regions.name: Adjara
regions.merged_summary:
Adjara is an autonomous Black Sea republic within Georgia, and the country's national regime applies here in full, with no local exception.

Batumi, the regional capital, is a resort and tourism hub where foreign visitors are a routine part of daily life; its tourism economy, hotel-driven hospitality culture and more cosmopolitan nightlife make everyday encounters less uniformly conservative than in many inland Georgian settings, and refusal of service by commercial staff is less likely. Outside the resort strip the picture shifts: Adjara's mixed Orthodox and Muslim population is socially conservative, with religiously influenced communities in rural highland villages and clerical influence that means visible gender nonconformity draws friction, while the region's sparse trans community infrastructure offers little local support or civic network to turn to.

Adjara's autonomy has produced no separate protective law, policing exception, documented enforcement practice or civic infrastructure distinguishing it from the national picture. Reported differences are modest and affect daily exposure rather than underlying risk: local police discretion and the absence of reliable remedies mean that discovery or visible nonconformity still carries real exposure to hostility with little dependable recourse, and there is no Adjara-specific record of enforcement either toward or against trans visitors. That gap in local records is not evidence of safety.

regions.name: Imereti
regions.merged_summary: Imereti is subject to Georgia's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is centred on Kutaisi, the country's third-largest city, but is largely rural, strongly Orthodox and more socially conservative than Tbilisi; beyond the tourist routes around Kutaisi's airport and nearby cave sites, anonymity is limited and LGBTI visibility is low, with no visible local trans community and few LGBTI-friendly services or advocacy groups compared with the capital. One locally documented incident stands out: far-right violence against an LGBT-linked venue in Kutaisi in 2023. There are no Imereti-specific raids or lethal enforcement beyond the national framework, and no evidence of organised targeting of foreign visitors, but the absence of safe local infrastructure means a trans visitor discovered in a hotel, clinic or police stop is more likely to face gossip, service refusal or hostility, with thinner police accountability and victim support than in Tbilisi. Recourse is weak: legal and health services are fewer, and enforcement that is already unreliable nationally is reported as harder to reach from Imereti's smaller, less networked cities.

regions.name: Ashanti Region
regions.merged_summary: Ashanti Region is subject to Ghana's national law in full, with no local exception. Local conditions shape how that regime is felt on the ground: the region is anchored by Kumasi, a major urban, commercial and tourist centre whose hotels and businesses afford foreign visitors some daily anonymity compared with rural areas, while the wider hinterland is dense with community surveillance. Authority is shared among evangelical and Pentecostal churches, Muslim communities and Asante chiefly institutions under the Asantehene, and hostility toward sexual and gender minorities is broadly socially licensed rather than confined to officials. Support infrastructure is thin — there is little of Accra's NGO, legal-aid or advocacy presence — and no region-specific protective practice or enforcement exception is known. Being identified as trans in a market, lorry station or Zongo neighbourhood can bring denunciation, denial of a room, transport scrutiny, hostile treatment in hospitals, eviction, extortion or mob confrontation, with police involvement more likely to escalate than to protect. Police and courts function, but complaints touching gender nonconformity are read through a morality lens and rarely produce a remedy for the person who is outed. Sparse local enforcement records mean the extent of trans-specific police targeting is uncertain locally, and that uncertainty is not evidence of safety. A historical Asante tradition of feminine-identified men exists, but it does not offset these risks.

regions.name: Central Region
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Ghana's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes the Central Region from the national picture for a transgender visitor. The region centres on Cape Coast and spans coastal and interior districts — a heritage-tourism and university corridor including Elmina where foreign visitors are routine, alongside fishing districts and smaller towns that are more tightly networked and socially conservative. Nothing documents a different local enforcement pattern, distinct police practice or local protection, and hotel, heritage-site or municipal encounters here are governed by the same national regime rather than any local accommodation; visitor-facing staff may avoid public disputes with foreigners, but that offers no documented safeguard for an outed trans traveller.

regions.name: Gibraltar
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Gibraltar's national law in full, with no local exception. Gibraltar is a single compact jurisdiction, so the territory-wide legal picture is what a visitor meets on the ground: British-style courts and policing operate in a small, English-speaking, tourist-facing place where visitors are routine, openly LGBT people are visible, and an annual Pride is held. Discretion is limited by the density of the territory — a close-knit, partly socially conservative community where a trans visitor is conspicuous and anonymity is scarce, so encounters in hotels, clinics and with police turn largely on the individuals involved. Friction, stares and the occasional service problem are the more plausible forms of difficulty here. The frontier with Spain is operated under Spanish procedures outside Gibraltar's control, so checks there are not governed by the territory's own institutions. No incidents of police targeting, facility exclusion or violence against trans visitors are documented in the material available for Gibraltar; equally, how officials handle document discrepancies, how the protections operate in practice, and current social attitudes toward trans visitors are not established — that gap should not be read as reassurance.

regions.name: Labe
regions.merged_summary: Labé is subject to Guinea's national law in full, with no local exception. Labé is Guinea's second-largest city, set in the Fouta Djallon highlands and predominantly Fulani and Muslim, where social and religious norms are stricter than in Conakry and visible gender nonconformity draws close scrutiny. Anonymity is harder to hold in a mid-size highland city than in the capital, and discovery could quickly involve relatives, local religious authorities or the police. Tourist infrastructure is limited, making a visibly transgender visitor more identifiable. Fewer independent services exist than in Conakry — fewer LGBTQ organisations, legal-aid options or anonymous urban spaces — and no local protection, functioning complaint mechanism or sanctuary is documented; family and religious pressure to conform remains strong. Region-specific police practice, treatment of trans visitors at entry points, and incidents involving trans travelers in Labé are not recorded, and that absence of evidence is not evidence of safety. Nothing local is documented that softens the national picture: weaker institutional presence, stricter social norms and closer community monitoring mean discovery is more likely to escalate, with limited recourse.

regions.name: Banjul
regions.merged_summary: Banjul is subject to Gambia's national regime in full, with no local exception or protective measure of its own. As the country's compact administrative capital and main Atlantic port, it concentrates police, immigration and government headquarters, so identity checks around the airport, ferry terminal and checkpoints are common and anonymity is limited for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor. The city is a devoutly Muslim, socially conservative place where LGBT identity carries strong taboo and no visible trans community infrastructure exists, and gender nonconformity may be read locally as sexual immorality or public nuisance — raising the risk of intrusive questioning, humiliation, extortion or arbitrary detention if a visitor is outed at documents, hotels, hospitals or through community reporting. Set against that, the capital's urban scale offers more anonymity than rural areas, some tourist-facing services, and a concentration of embassies, NGOs and civil-society organisations that may improve consular access after a detention. The nearby tourism corridor across the ferry in Kanifing is accustomed to foreign visitors, and enforcement there is sporadic rather than systematic; however, occasional police sweeps of venues and couples have occurred in living memory, and no documented local tolerance, lighter enforcement or effective remedy distinguishes Banjul from the national picture.

regions.name: Basse
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Gambia's national law in full, with no local exception. Basse (Basse Santa Su) is the small administrative, trading and transport hub of the inland Upper River Region in the east of the country, close to the Senegalese border. It is a predominantly rural, tightly knit, Muslim-majority town with little tourism infrastructure, few health and lodging providers, and only limited NGO, legal-aid or oversight presence; courts and advocacy groups are distant, and religious and traditional authorities carry more practical weight than institutions in Banjul. A foreign transgender visitor is conspicuous, and news tends to travel quickly through family, market and mosque networks, so discovery carries a real risk of public shaming, service refusal, extortion, informal mediation or police detention rather than formal protection. The nearby border crossing adds document scrutiny on top of everyday encounters with officials. Nothing indicates local tolerance, a sanctuary policy, or trans-aware enforcement practice, and no documented Basse-specific pattern of police targeting or violence against transgender visitors has been established — that absence of evidence should not be read as safety, and the treatment a visitor would actually receive from local officials remains uncertain. Remote geography and weaker accountability mean national provisions can operate with greater local discretion than in larger cities.

regions.name: Brikama
regions.merged_summary: Brikama is subject to Gambia's national law in full, with no local exception. Brikama is a large, densely settled Mandinka-majority market town in the West Coast Region, built around markets, mosques, schools and local administration, lying inland from the more international tourism strip along the coast — the nearby resorts offer some familiarity with foreign visitors and a degree of anonymity around lodging, but Brikama itself has far less tourism infrastructure than Banjul or Senegambia. Local society is socially and religiously conservative and Muslim-majority, and less accustomed to foreign gender-nonconforming visitors: a visibly trans person draws attention, and stop-and-question by police, hotel staff or bystanders is plausible. Discovery can lead to document-mismatch scrutiny at checks, questioning or refusal of service, and extortion is a realistic risk; resort anonymity does not extend to official encounters. Local policing operates within the national morality framework, so a visitor who is identified faces the same criminal exposure as elsewhere in Gambia, but with less anonymity and less likely assistance. No local support, health or legal services for transgender people are known, and no local ordinance, practice or protective mechanism is documented. At the same time, no localised record of violence or enforcement specific to trans travellers is available, so neither local tolerance nor local severity should be assumed, and no reliable remedy is documented locally.

regions.name: Janjanbureh
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Gambia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Janjanbureh is a small, comparatively remote riverain town on MacCarthy Island in the Gambia River, within the Central River Region — inland, less internationally oriented, and far from the coastal visitor belt around Banjul. Tourism infrastructure is limited, as are legal-aid, advocacy and LGBT support services, so a trans visitor has thinner practical backing than on the coast. The town is small, rural and Muslim-majority, with strong conservative religious authority and tight social networks: anonymity is scarce, a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor draws attention quickly, and any discovery can spread fast through family, community leaders and police contacts. Rural policing and informal local authority add unpredictability to encounters with officials, and there are no documented local protections, complaint mechanisms or facility protocols that offset the national regime; local officials are unlikely to be a dependable source of protection. Social pressure around identity and privacy can extend to families.

No Janjanbureh-specific reports of targeting or of tolerance were identified, and no local exception or protective practice distinguishes the town from the national picture — but that absence of local evidence is not evidence of safety. Local isolation, limited visitor support and reduced anonymity compound concern relative to the national baseline.

regions.name: Kanifing
regions.merged_summary: Kanifing is subject to Gambia's national law in full, with no local exception. Kanifing Municipality is the country's densest urban and most tourism-exposed district, encompassing Serekunda, Kololi and the Senegambia strip in the Greater Banjul area adjoining the capital. The transient, internationally exposed population of the coastal tourism corridor — hospitality workers, NGOs, expatriates and visiting foreigners — gives a gender-nonconforming visitor more anonymity and somewhat greater everyday tolerance of nonconforming presentation than in rural areas, so casual, village-level scrutiny is lower. That moderation is limited: police operate from urban stations, hotel registration is routine, and the airport is close at hand, so anonymity does not extend to official encounters. Police and intelligence attention to queer and gender-nonconforming people has historically concentrated in this urban corridor, where extortion and arbitrary detention without effective remedy are documented risks. Social conservatism remains strong across the municipality, and the tourist economy does not translate into legal protection; no local sanctuary, tolerance programme or other protective measure distinguishing Kanifing from the national picture was identified. Urbanity therefore offers cover rather than shelter — local conditions lower the chance of casual exposure but do not soften what follows once discovery draws official attention, and no established pattern of enforcement against trans visitors specifically has been documented here.

regions.name: Kerewan
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Gambia's national law in full, with no local exception. Kerewan is a small administrative and market centre on the North Bank, reached by ferry and surrounded by farmland rather than resorts, with a predominantly Mandinka, Muslim population and only a handful of hotels, clinics and legal-aid services compared with the Banjul coast. That shape matters for a trans visitor. Foreign visitors are conspicuous here: there is no tourist or expatriate enclave to disappear into, no visible trans community, advocacy group or safe venue, and community and religious leaders carry weight in how gender nonconformity is read. Anonymity is thin — discovery tends to come through lodging registration, documents, or simply being noticed in a close-knit town where gossip travels quickly. Local discretion sits with thinly staffed police and community gatekeepers rather than with courts, so harassment, extortion or brief detention are more plausible outcomes of being outed than formal proceedings; at the same time, the practical support that might follow is thinner than in Banjul or the tourist south, with fewer alternative places to stay, medical options, legal aid, consular reach and international monitoring. Family and community outing therefore carries more consequence here than in a hub where a visitor can melt away. No local ordinance, protection or institutional exception distinguishing Kerewan from the national picture was identified, and no distinct trans-targeted enforcement campaign is documented locally.

regions.name: Kuntaur
regions.merged_summary: Kuntaur lies within Gambia's national regime in full, with no local exception.
