No Miyagi-specific law targeting transgender visitors, no local pattern of police targeting or trans-targeted violence, and no prefectural or municipal protection delivering redress to a short-term visitor are documented; how an individual facility handles a trans guest remains uncertain.

regions.name: Osaka Prefecture
regions.merged_summary:
Osaka Prefecture is subject to Japan's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a large, densely urban and heavily visited prefecture whose social texture differs from the national picture: Osaka city has a visible, established LGBTQ commercial district centred on Doyamacho and the Namba/Horie area, described as Japan's largest, alongside a tourism and nightlife economy in Namba and Shinsaibashi that is accustomed to visible difference, and municipal partnership certificates have been issued since 2016. Everyday encounters here read as relaxed rather than reserved, so a trans visitor is more likely to meet indifference than hostility, and LGBTQ-oriented venues and private-bath options are easier to find than in smaller cities.

None of this is a legal safeguard: partnership certificates do not protect a visitor, and visibility does not establish trans-specific acceptance. The friction a visitor actually meets is institutional — bathhouses and other gendered facilities, hotel front desks and ward-office counters where presentation and papers differ, and any police or immigration contact. No prefectural hostility, facility ban, or pattern of police targeting or trans-specific violence against trans visitors is documented locally, but limited regional documentation of enforcement should not be read as safety. Local rules on facilities and police conduct do not depart from the national picture, so exposure here is essentially the national one, within a somewhat more open everyday social environment.

regions.name: Saitama
regions.merged_summary: Saitama is subject to Japan's national framework in full, with no local exception. The prefecture sits immediately north of Tokyo in the dense metropolitan commuter belt: largely urban and suburban, with ordinary city services and heavy day-trip traffic toward the capital, but little standalone tourism of its own. Several assessments describe conservative, family-oriented social attitudes and less of the anonymity and international-service familiarity a visitor finds in central Tokyo, so a trans person who is out may meet staring, misgendering, intrusive questioning or refusal at some bathing and accommodation venues; the likely outcome is social friction and service exclusion rather than arrest or custody. There is no documented pattern of police targeting, organised hostility or violence against transgender visitors in the prefecture, and no prefecture-specific legislation, facility rule or enforcement practice aimed at transgender visitors is known. Visibility is uneven across the prefecture: Saitama City, Omiya and Kawaguchi are recorded as having same-sex partnership schemes and local human-rights ordinances that acknowledge sexual orientation and gender identity, suggesting somewhat better visibility and service availability than the national average, while the more rural western and northern areas are less LGBTQ-facing. LGBTQ-friendly venue guides circulate as private-sector alternatives. Bathhouse access and the handling of mismatched foreign identity documents at hotels and municipal offices remain uncertain in practice, and no local measure softens the institutional friction a trans visitor would meet elsewhere in Japan.

regions.name: Shiga
regions.merged_summary: Shiga Prefecture is subject to Japan's national legal framework in full, with no local exception and no added local protection. Shiga is a quiet, low-crime prefecture organised around Lake Biwa, the city of Otsu, shrines and lakeside resort areas; it is semi-rural and far less metropolitan than Tokyo or Osaka, and its tourism is largely domestic. No local ordinance, targeted violence, or pattern of police attention toward trans visitors has been documented here, and nothing local was found that would strengthen the national position either. What differs from the metropolitan picture is supply and familiarity: LGBTQ-friendly venues, private-bath alternatives and English-language guidance are thinner than in nearby Kyoto and Osaka, both reachable for day trips, while everyday contact rests more on reserved social attitudes and unfamiliarity than on any documented acceptance. In smaller lakeside and onsen communities, ryokan and bathhouse staff may respond awkwardly to a trans guest, ask intrusive questions, or decline service, with discretion varying sharply by establishment. The realistic local risks are social friction, misgendering, invasive curiosity and service refusal rather than arrest or violence.

regions.name: Tochigi
regions.merged_summary: Tochigi is an inland prefecture in northern Honshu, with Utsunomiya as its main city and the Nikko temple complex as its principal visitor draw; the region is subject to Japan's national law in full, with no local exception.

regions.name: Tokyo
regions.merged_summary:
Tokyo is subject to Japan's national regime in full, with no local exception. It is the country's most internationally visible and tourism-facing metropolis, with a large, anonymous urban fabric and a concentrated LGBTQ presence — Shinjuku Ni-chome is the country's largest district, with further venues in Shibuya and Roppongi — alongside hospitality and medical staff more accustomed to gender diversity than in most of Japan. Short-stay visitors generally find public life reserved and low in confrontation, and more private rooms, private-bath options and gender-neutral facilities are available here than in smaller communities. Ordinary disclosure is more likely to produce curiosity, misgendering, service friction or a bathhouse refusal than official attention, though an arrest or medical emergency can escalate matters sharply.

Local measures exist but read as climate rather than protection: Tokyo has run a partnership certificate system since 2016 and adopted a 2018 metropolitan ordinance on respect for gender identity and sexual orientation in prefectural administration. Neither functions as a remedy for a visitor, and no shield-type protection against discrimination is documented here; remedies that exist are slow. Everyday comfort does not extend to encounters administered nationally — immigration, official document handling and detention remain outside metropolitan practice, as does placement in gendered facilities by registered record — so document checks, onsen and sento use and local office paperwork can still force disclosure and denial. No trans-specific targeting of visitors and no local violence pattern are documented; that absence should not be read as safety.

regions.name: North Kazakhstan Region
regions.merged_summary: North Kazakhstan Region falls entirely under Kazakhstan's national regime, with no local exception of its own. The region is rural, agricultural and largely Russian-speaking, with a more conservative social climate and far less visible LGBTQ support infrastructure than Almaty or Astana. Beyond that, no region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this region from the national picture, and local enforcement practice here is undocumented. That absence of reporting should not be read as safety: where local conditions are unrecorded, the country-level information is all a visitor has to plan by, and the scarcity of nearby support means any difficulty encountered would be harder to resolve than in the larger cities.

regions.name: South Kazakhstan Region
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kazakhstan's national law in full, with no local exception. South Kazakhstan Region — centred on Turkestan and Shymkent, now administered as Turkistan Region — is more socially traditional, religiously observant and rural than Almaty or Astana, with less international exposure and a far thinner network of advocacy and trans-specific services. LGBTQ visibility is very low, and informal support is easiest to find only within Shymkent's university and student milieu. Practically, the national regime described at country level meets an environment in which gender diversity is unfamiliar to much of the public and to police officers. A trans visitor who is recognised or outed may face refusal of services, questioning, harassment or extortion, with strong family and community norms making outing a live concern and hotel or clinic encounters awkward; police discretion can be harsher and less predictable than in the major cities, and how national rules would be applied to a trans visitor here is genuinely uncertain. No region-specific pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence has been recorded for the area, but that reflects limited documentation rather than evidence of safety — there is no documented local protective practice to fall back on, and recourse after an incident is weak.

regions.name: Kajiado
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kenya's national law in full, with no local exception. Kajiado is a Maasai-majority, socially conservative county: its northern towns of Kitengela, Ongata Rongai and Ngong sit in the Nairobi commuter belt, and Amboseli's tourism economy draws steady foreign visitor traffic — an urban and tourist fringe offering more anonymity than rural areas, where customary patriarchal gender norms and small-town visibility can expose an outed visitor to scrutiny, with little trans-specific support outside limited Nairobi-linked networks. Beyond this, no region-specific evidence was found distinguishing Kajiado from the national picture on entry, policing, facilities or healthcare; no county ordinance or pattern of documented targeting is recorded, which reflects an absence of local records rather than a measure of safety.

regions.name: Kiambu
regions.merged_summary:
Kiambu County is subject to Kenya's national law and policing in full, with no local exception.

Wrapping around Nairobi's northern and eastern edges, Kiambu is a densely populated commuter belt of dormitory and market towns — Thika, Ruiru, Juja, Kikuyu and Limuru — with a largely Kikuyu, strongly Christian social environment and a more agricultural, small-town interior. A visibly gender-nonconforming visitor generally finds more anonymity here than in upcountry rural Kenya, and Nairobi-based legal and advocacy support is within easy reach; however, the anonymity of the crowd does not extend to encounters with police, county hospitals or document offices, where national institutions decide the outcome. Small-town and market-centre policing remains socially conservative, and rural and church-influenced areas are the least forgiving. No Kiambu county ordinance, policing directive or documented trans-specific incident was identified, and neither the local police stations nor the county hospitals offer trans-specific recourse, so a visitor who is outed or stopped faces the same local police and social exposure as elsewhere in Kenya.

The absence of county records should not be read as evidence of tolerance or lighter enforcement: no local immunity or differing intensity of practice in Kiambu has been established either way.

regions.name: Lamu
regions.merged_summary:
Lamu is subject to Kenya's national legal regime in full, with no local exception.

Lamu is a small, tightly knit, predominantly Muslim Swahili coastal community spread across an archipelago of island towns including Lamu Old Town and Shella. Conservative religious and social norms carry strong force: modest dress is customarily expected, strict public gender norms and gender-segregated practices shape daily life, and gender nonconformity draws immediate public notice in close-knit public spaces. Anonymity is far more limited than in Nairobi or Mombasa, and discovery would likely spread quickly through the community. Kadhi courts administer Muslim personal status matters on the islands, and there is no LGBTI advocacy organisation, community venue, or specialised medical or legal-aid service locally; support of any kind is distant.

The tourism economy softens everyday dealings with foreigners and lends visitor areas a degree of informal tolerance, but the buffer is thin: hotel and boat staff seeking to avoid scandal may invite scrutiny, and document checks on arrival and on movement by ferry or air mean a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming visitor stands out both as a foreigner and as gender-nonconforming. Local police and authorities have historically been responsive to moral and religious pressure in coastal counties, so a complaint against a visitor could be met with detention, bribe demands or public humiliation rather than protection, with little practical access to legal recourse. Al-Shabaab-linked insecurity in the wider county further thins ordinary state presence, though it is a general security risk rather than one aimed at trans people. No organised lethal targeting is documented here, and no local safeguard, protective practice or distinct rule distinguishing Lamu from the national picture has been identified — local frequency of harm is uncertain rather than absent.

regions.name: Machakos
regions.merged_summary:
Machakos County lies wholly within Kenya's national legal regime, with no local exception of its own. It sits immediately southeast of Nairobi, centred on Machakos town and Athi River, and is largely rural and peri-urban: a closely knit, socially conservative, predominantly Christian Kamba area with strong church influence and little anonymity for a visibly foreign or gender-nonconforming visitor.

No county-level protective ordinance, trans organising or specialist local service infrastructure is known here, and county courts and hospitals are less accustomed to gender-identity disputes than their Nairobi counterparts — so a passport check, incident report or medical request that draws attention may raise the odds of misgendered custody, shakedowns or refused service. Legal and NGO recourse runs through Nairobi-based lawyers and organisations rather than anything local. In everyday terms, difficulty in Machakos is more likely to surface as gossip, refused service, police shakedowns or short detention than as prosecution for identity itself; the county's thin civic space and low anonymity, rather than any local legal difference, are what set it apart from the capital. Most documented harassment cases in the national record come from Nairobi and Mombasa, and Machakos has no comparable body of local documentation — a gap in recording, not evidence that nothing occurs.

regions.name: Narok
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kenya's national law in full, with no local exception. Narok is a largely rural, Maasai-majority county in southwestern Kenya on the Tanzania border, shaped by pastoralist communities and the Maasai Mara safari circuit rather than by any urban centre. Its main visitor economy runs through international lodges and tour operators, which can offer comparatively discreet, tourist-tolerant settings; lodge employment and the safari corridor give guests some practical shelter, but not a protective system. Away from that corridor, transit through Narok town and Kilgoris is not shielded: the county has a small-town, strongly patriarchal character in which visibly gender-nonconforming strangers attract immediate public attention, and conservative customary norms and rigid gender expectations mean that a visitor outed outside tourist enclaves may face community confrontation, elder or public humiliation, and crowd exposure. Maasai customary traditions of gender-variant roles offer some local familiarity but carry no legal protection. County policing in rural areas is thinner and more discretionary than in the capital, and courts, legal aid and LGBT advocacy networks based in Nairobi, Nakuro and Mombasa are a long way off, weakening any practical remedy. Narok has no documented local protective ordinance, LGBT organisation or trans-specific services, and no region-specific reports of incidents involving trans visitors are known — an absence of local documentation is not evidence of safety. Local conditions may intensify exposure beyond what the national record describes, particularly in remote areas.

regions.name: Tana River
regions.merged_summary: Tana River is subject to Kenya's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a sparsely populated, largely rural strip along the lower Tana, dominated by pastoralist communities with strong clan and religious authority and a significant Muslim population; it sees few tourists and has little visitor-facing infrastructure. Compared with Nairobi and Mombasa, policing is thinner, court and legal-aid access is limited, and LGBTQ and civil-society support structures are largely absent, so the national court-driven protections and association rights operate here mainly on paper, mediated by officials who may be isolated from oversight. A discovered trans visitor would more likely be confronted by local police, health workers or community members than by any institution with contact with national advocacy or legal networks, and communal exposure can carry social consequences beyond any official encounter. The county also has a history of periodic intercommunal violence, adding to a general background of local insecurity. Distance from the capital and the coast means that whatever remedy exists nationally is practically hard to reach from here, and a visitor's own networks, transport options and documentation access should be planned on the assumption that local recourse will be slow or unavailable. No county-specific record of anti-trans incidents, and no local protective ordinance or service provision, was identified — this reflects the absence of documented local evidence rather than an indication of safety, and conditions in Tana River should not be inferred from the better-documented urban picture.

regions.name: Uasin Gishu
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kenya's national law in full, with no local exception. Uasin Gishu is a Rift Valley highland county built around Eldoret, a sizeable university and hospital town whose institutions, medical complex and crowds give a trans visitor a measure of day-to-day anonymity that smaller settlements around it do not. Beyond Eldoret's urban centre the county turns quickly to farming country, where privacy is thinner, church influence on gender questions is stronger, and an outed visitor is more likely to draw a crowd or a public confrontation. The county has no recorded anti-discrimination ordinance, shelter, trans-specific advocacy group or other visitor-facing protection of its own, so practical support tends to depend on national organisations at a distance from Eldoret and on the discretion of local officers. Eldoret's High Court has issued a protective ruling for a trans petitioner held in custody here, which shows the county's judiciary will entertain such claims, but it is a slow route rather than a working remedy: no changed custody, policing or service practice follows from it on the ground, and discovery can still mean intrusive questioning, detention and hostile conditions before any court is reached. Overall conditions sit close to the national picture, with strong local conservatism and thin support infrastructure cutting slightly against safety and the presence of a functioning High Court offering only a partial, delayed check.

regions.name: Chuy Region
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Kyrgyzstan's national law in full, with no local exception. Chuy Region rings the capital Bishkek and takes in Tokmok, Kant and the Manas International Airport corridor, making it the country's most urbanised, Russian-speaking and transit-oriented area, with busy Kazakh border crossings to the north. Most visitors arrive through this gateway, and in practice discovery of a trans visitor here tends to happen at the airport, at land borders, in hotels, clinics or small conservative towns rather than through formal legal process; the outcomes reported are harassment, service refusal, privacy exposure and possible extortion or police trouble rather than arrest. The capital's remaining community and NGO networks, together with the anonymity of a partly foreign-facing transit area, offer somewhat more discretion than rural southern parts of the country, but public LGBTQ venues in the wider capital area have largely disappeared, and police and social hostility remain the main risks if a visitor is outed. Outside the capital's immediate area the Chuy valley is rural, agricultural and markedly more conservative, with fear of family and community ostracism reported as especially acute there and fewer protective networks available. Anonymity gained through a port of entry or a hotel stay does not extend to official encounters.

regions.name: Preah Sihanouk
regions.merged_summary:
Preah Sihanouk is subject to Cambodia's national law in full, with no local exception. The province centres on Sihanoukville, Cambodia's main coastal port and a beach resort that has shifted toward casino and construction tourism, with a transient foreign population, a dense guesthouse and nightlife economy, and substantial informal entertainment work.

No local statute, ordinance, facility rule or protective measure specific to trans visitors has been documented, and there is no local incident record that distinguishes the province from the national picture — an absence of evidence, not evidence of safety. Resort districts are accustomed to foreign visitors, and ordinary hotel, beach and nightlife settings attract little identity scrutiny, which offers some buffer. Against that, the post-2019 casino-and-compound boom left a weakly accountable policing environment in which extortion of vulnerable visitors is a known pattern, alongside wider corruption and organised-crime concerns, and police treatment of transgender entertainment workers follows national patterns. There is no Pride parade or LGBT venue infrastructure comparable to Phnom Penh or Siem Reap, leaving fewer local advocates and less established tolerant nightlife, so discovery depends more on private hospitality staff, checkpoints or crime-associated settings.

Conditional on discovery, the likely outcomes are gossip, service refusal, extortion or humiliation rather than prosecution; border treatment, facility access and police responses remain uncertain, and local recourse is thin.

regions.name: Siem Reap
regions.merged_summary:
Siem Reap is governed by Cambodia's national framework in full, with no local legal exception.

The province's economy is built almost entirely on tourism: a large hotel and hospitality sector, international-standard accommodation and a visible bar and club scene mean that ordinary customer-facing contact is markedly more relaxed toward visibly gender-nonconforming and same-sex travellers than in less international parts of the country. The documented local police conduct recorded by Cambodian rights researchers, however, concerned transgender sex workers specifically, so the clearest abuse on record sits in sex-work enforcement rather than in visitor settings. That evidence is now dated, and current local policing practice and the remedies actually available are unclear — an absence of reporting should not be read as an absence of risk. Where exposure does arise for a traveller it is most likely to come from discretionary police contact: gender-marker or document mismatches, questioning, detention or demands for money, particularly away from the hotel and nightlife crowds where social tolerance is highest. Street harassment of visibly gender-nonconforming people is also recorded in the city. Practical welcome is therefore strongest inside the tourism bubble and weakest at its edges, where social goodwill offers no protection against official conduct.

regions.name: Line Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Line Islands fall under Kiribati's national regime in full, with no local exception. What sets them apart is geography: remote eastern atolls centred on Kiritimati (London), a scatter of tiny, tightly knit and socially conservative Christian communities where a foreign visitor stands out, word travels fast, and privacy after any disclosure is effectively unavailable. Kiritimati's resort and fishing economy, along with its historic military and scientific presence, make outsiders relatively familiar there, while the smaller atolls are quieter and less used to visitors.

What a trans visitor is likely to encounter is exposure rather than official action. Health and police services are thin, there are no trans-specific services or discreet care infrastructure, and serious cases may require evacuation to Tarawa or abroad, so outside help is slow to arrive and formal complaint routes are weak. Recognised as transgender, a visitor can expect curiosity, gossip, moral disapproval, harassment or refusal of service, settled informally through community pressure with little remedy. No distinct local law or protective practice is known, and there is no record of targeted anti-trans violence or police campaigns in the islands; because trans-specific local evidence is thin, that silence should not be read as assurance.

regions.name: Phoenix Islands
regions.merged_summary:
The Phoenix Islands lie fully within Kiribati's national legal framework, with no separate local regime.

The group is a remote, largely uninhabited atoll chain: Kanton is the only settled island, with a few dozen residents and a small government station, and there is no police post, court, clinic, or tourism infrastructure. Access is generally by permit or research vessel, and most of the islands serve conservation and research uses, with only occasional small-scale eco-tourism and research visits. No region-specific pattern of targeting, hostility, or restrictive practice toward trans visitors is documented, but that absence of local evidence is not evidence of safety: current local attitudes are unknown, Kiribati's binabinaaine tradition offers some cultural familiarity with gender-variant people, and the only national observation of the social climate is a decade old.

Practically, any stay makes discovery close to certain in a tiny, strongly Christian community, where misgendering, gossip, informal scrutiny, and refusal of services are more plausible outcomes than official action — there is no local enforcement presence on hand to detain or prosecute. The main drawback is what follows discovery: with no clinic, legal advice, or redress mechanism on the islands, an incident would depend on distant authorities in Tarawa and on evacuation, whose limits apply in so remote a setting. A trans visitor leaves with essentially no local remedy.

regions.name: Christ Church Nichola Town
regions.merged_summary: Christ Church Nichola Town is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish is a small, largely rural community on Nevis with modest tourism, and the island's small population limits a visibly trans visitor's anonymity. No region-specific evidence was found distinguishing this parish from the national picture: no local legislation, enforcement practice, official posture or incident record concerning transgender visitors has been documented here, so conditions in the parish track those described at country level.

regions.name: Saint Anne Sandy Point
regions.merged_summary: Saint Anne Sandy Point is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this parish from the national picture for a trans visitor: no documented local incidents, parish-level officials, or separate practices appear in the record, and the absence of recorded local hostility should not be read as safety. The parish is a small, quiet, mostly residential town on Saint Kitts's northwest peninsula, a short distance north of Basseterre and the main airport and near the Brimstone Hill historic site, with little tourism infrastructure. Its close-knit, church-oriented character means a visitor who is recognised is more likely to face gossip, staring and social disapproval than in Basseterre, with limited anonymous space in which to manage that attention.

regions.name: Saint George Basseterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint George Basseterre is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish contains Basseterre, the capital and the country's principal cruise and air gateway, along with the cruise terminal, most hotels, government offices and the concentration of tourist services and an expatriate community — an urban, visitor-facing setting where foreign faces are routine and encounters are commercial and anonymous rather than village-based. Local society remains socially conservative, and nothing in the parish adds protection beyond the national framework. The best-known official exclusion of LGBTQ visitors, a 2005 cruise ship barred from docking, happened at Nevis's port rather than Basseterre's, and no comparable barring of visitors has been documented here; no trans-specific local statute, checkpoint rule or documented incident involving a trans visitor distinguishes the parish. In practice, exposure is most likely to arise in service, accommodation or commercial encounters, or in discretionary interactions with officials at the port or in the city, where a conservative setting can produce service refusal, harassment or indifference with no local avenue for remedy. The capital's market-facing tourism economy makes heavy-handed treatment of paying visitors unlikely, but visitor-facing friendliness should not be read as local acceptance, and no local operating protection is documented for a trans person who is outed or needs help here.

regions.name: Saint George Gingerland
regions.merged_summary: Saint George Gingerland is a small, mainly rural parish on Nevis, governed by Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. It is an agricultural, village-based parish with no resorts or nightlife strip, and no parish-specific ordinance, protective measure or documented incident distinguishes it from the wider island picture. Local conditions shape how the national regime is actually felt: the close-knit community and the visibility of outsiders mean a gender-nonconforming or openly trans visitor is likely to be noticed and identified, with little anonymity; lodging and medical options are few, and both everyday services and police response are thinner than on Saint Kitts, so help is harder to obtain if something goes wrong. Nevis has a locally documented signal on official posture: in 2005 the island's port authority barred an LGBTQ cruise ship and announced the exclusion publicly as a cultural decision, stating that homosexuality was not part of Nevis's culture. No trans-specific criminal penalty for presentation is known and no organized violence campaign is recorded, so the main exposure if discovered is social disapproval, humiliation, refused service and isolation rather than arrest — though no parish-level protective machinery operates, and facility, custody or care practices at parish level are simply undocumented.

regions.name: Saint James Windward
regions.merged_summary: Saint James Windward is a small, rural parish on Nevis, subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. Its economy rests on resort and estate tourism — Golden Rock and the Pinney's Beach properties — alongside tight-knit village communities, so a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is quickly noticed and gossip travels fast; the anonymity a traveller might expect in a rural Caribbean setting is thin here. No parish-level protective measures, local ordinances or hospitality-sector guarantees are known, and civility from resort staff is informal rather than enforceable. No parish-specific trans-targeting, document checks or facility restrictions are documented, but the absence of such records should not be read as evidence of safety in a parish with limited institutions and no local support infrastructure. Nevis carries the federation's only documented official exclusion gesture: in 2005 port authorities turned away a cruise ship carrying a mostly LGBTQ passenger list, announcing the decision publicly as a defence of island culture. The episode is two decades old and does not establish routine current targeting, but it is the clearest local signal of an official willingness to exclude on cultural grounds, and it marks formal, documented encounters — ports, immigration, official business — as the points where local posture surfaces rather than dissolves. A visitor whose identity becomes known in these small communities may face gossip, social hostility or service refusal with thin practical recourse, leaving the combined local picture marginally less favourable than the national baseline.

regions.name: Saint John Capisterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint John Capisterre is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish is a small, rural area on northern Saint Kitts taking in Dieppe Bay, Saddler and St. Paul's, with little tourism infrastructure and a close-knit population in which a trans visitor's anonymity is limited. Nothing found here distinguishes the region from the national picture: there is no documented local protection for trans visitors, and no documented organised local targeting. That absence of local evidence should not be read as safety — parish life means discovery is likely to become socially visible, discreet services are scarce, and recourse after harassment or refusal of service is thin, with sympathetic services or legal support generally meaning travel to Basseterre. Current local treatment and remedies remain uncertain.

regions.name: Saint John Figtree
regions.merged_summary:
Saint John Figtree is a small parish settlement on Nevis, though some accounts place it on Saint Kitts near Basseterre; either way it is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions, rather than any separate local rule, shape a visit here. The parish is small, rural and socially conservative, with a strongly religious community, so a visibly transgender visitor is unlikely to remain anonymous: gossip, misgendering and informal service friction are the most plausible difficulties, and an identity that becomes known in a community of this size tends to follow a visitor between businesses, churches and transport. Nevis's tourism-dependent economy — Charlestown's port, resort districts and reliance on outside visitors — encourages everyday hospitality and informal tolerance in commercial settings; that anonymity does not extend to official encounters, where the island's posture toward LGBTQ visitors has been less welcoming, and border questioning or refusal of admission remains possible in exceptional cases. No local protective machinery, distinct local enforcement pattern, or documented trans-specific violence is known, and severe punishment is not documented. The practical effect is that difficulty in Saint John Figtree is more likely to be social than criminal, with no local remedy if it hardens into refusal of service or harassment.

regions.name: Saint Mary Cayon
regions.merged_summary: Saint Mary Cayon is a small coastal parish on the central part of Saint Kitts, outside the main tourist belt around Basseterre and Frigate Bay, where a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor could attract informal scrutiny in a close-knit, small-community setting. The parish is subject to the national regime of Saint Kitts and Nevis in full, with no local exception. No region-specific information distinguishes Saint Mary Cayon from the national picture: no parish-specific law, campaign, or protective measure is known, and nothing has been documented locally either way — no record of targeting, and no record of local support or remedy. Outcomes for a visitor here would rest on individual encounters rather than any known local pattern.

regions.name: Saint Paul Capisterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint Paul Capisterre is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. It is a small, rural parish on the northern coast of Saint Kitts, within easy reach of Basseterre and the island's main port, airport and tourist services, but with little tourist traffic of its own and no LGBTQ-specific venues, support services or advocacy groups locally. The population is tight-knit and church-going, and a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor would likely be read as an outsider: in a community of this size word travels quickly, and discretion and anonymity are much harder to maintain than in Basseterre or the tourist belt. Social friction, and attention during document checks, are the realistic exposure rather than any dedicated local enforcement. Policing is thin, and nothing in the parish — no separate local law, facility rule or border practice — modifies the national regime. The 2005 exclusion of an LGBTQ cruise ship took place at Nevis, not on Saint Kitts, so it signals past official cultural wariness at entry points rather than a Saint Kitts or parish practice. No local incidents of anti-trans violence or state targeting are documented here, and that gap reflects missing local information rather than any established safety.

regions.name: Saint Paul Charlestown
regions.merged_summary: Saint Paul Charlestown is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. Charlestown is the small capital and main port of Nevis, the smaller and socially more conservative of the two islands, and a close-knit parish in a tourism-dependent economy built on resorts and visiting yachts. The 2005 refusal to let an LGBTQ cruise ship dock in Nevis was issued from this port in the name of local culture: a dated incident that marks official and social conservatism at the point of entry, though it does not establish how often such hostility occurs today. Everyday exposure is moderated by the hospitality economy, where tourist-facing commerce tends to be pragmatic, but in a town of this size a trans visitor's visibility is higher and discovery carries greater social consequence than in a larger setting; the most plausible forms of friction are bureaucratic or service refusals, discomfort in a close-knit community, and weak recourse if harassment occurs. Medical and support services are limited, and St Kitts-based organisations are a journey away, so there is little protective infrastructure on hand. No region-specific protections, tourist-tolerance exceptions, or trans-specific border or facility restrictions are documented for the parish, and the record contains no documented local pattern of trans-specific violence or targeting; that silence reflects limited documentation rather than verified safety.

regions.name: Saint Peter Basseterre
regions.merged_summary: Saint Peter Basseterre is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish contains Basseterre, the federal capital and the country's principal cruise-port and air-entry point — the Robert L. Bradshaw International Airport, the city's eastern suburbs and the Frigate Bay resort belt all fall within it — so document checks, immigration questioning and port discretion are concentrated here more than in any rural parish, and every visitor passes through its screening. Everyday conditions are shaped by a tourism-dependent, service-oriented economy: hotels, restaurants and cruise traffic make the capital more anonymous and its staff more accustomed to foreign guests, and exposure to international visitors suggests somewhat more casual tolerance than the federation's more conservative fringes. The contrast within the parish is real, however: the inland villages around St. Peter's are small, church-centred and socially conservative, and casual friction is likelier there than along the waterfront. Basseterre's own port has no record of the kind of exclusion seen elsewhere in the federation — the documented 2005 refusal of an LGBTQ cruise ship was a Nevis decision, not this parish's. No trans-specific violence, organised local hostility, facility rule or local ordinance granting or denying protection is recorded for Saint Peter Basseterre; that silence reflects an absence of local reporting rather than a guarantee, and a visitor who is outed here should not assume a remedy available locally.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Lowland
regions.merged_summary: The parish falls under Saint Kitts and Nevis's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. Saint Thomas Lowland is a rural, low-density parish on Nevis, a small, churchgoing island society of roughly twelve thousand people, where a trans visitor who is outed becomes highly visible and privacy is limited — word travels quickly in a community of this size. Its upscale resort economy, serving international guests, works in the visitor's favour, offering comparatively neutral private settings and hospitality staff used to serving foreign travellers. Foreseeable difficulties here are social rather than official: refusals of lodging or service, questioning during entry or port arrangements, misgendering, and weak follow-up after an incident. Nevis's entry point carries the island's only recorded instance of official exclusion aimed at LGBTQ travellers; that incident is dated and does not establish current or routine targeting of trans visitors, but it remains the clearest public signal of how officials on this island have framed the question. How local officials would handle a mismatch between a foreign identity document and a visitor's presentation is undocumented, and no parish-specific border, facility, custody or violence practice is on record. No organised targeting or custodial risk has been documented locally, though the island's small scale means any incident is unlikely to pass unnoticed.

regions.name: Saint Thomas Middle Island
regions.merged_summary: Saint Thomas Middle Island is subject to Saint Kitts and Nevis national law in full, with no local exception. The parish is a rural stretch of Saint Kitts's west coast around Middle Island, Sandy Point and Half Way Tree, taking in visitor sites such as Romney Manor and Caribelle Batik; its small, tightly knit communities leave little anonymity for a visibly transgender visitor, everyday encounters at guesthouses, bars and village shops turn on informal discretion, and police and social services are thinner than in Basseterre. No parish-level ordinance, facility policy, incident record or enforcement practice distinguishes Saint Thomas Middle Island from the national picture, and the lack of local reports should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Trinity Palmetto Point
regions.merged_summary: Trinity Palmetto Point is subject to the Saint Kitts and Nevis national regime in full, with no local exception. The parish lies on Saint Kitts near Basseterre, taking in resort, villa and yachting-style visitor accommodation within a small, close-knit and socially conservative community where guests are served by neighbours and local staff rather than moving through anonymous tourism infrastructure. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Trinity Palmetto Point from the national picture, and that absence of local detail should not be read as added safety: the conditions described at country level apply here unchanged, and no parish-level protective service, remedy or documented pattern of targeting is known.

regions.name: Bokeo
regions.merged_summary: Bokeo is subject to Laos's national legal regime in full, with no local exception. The province occupies Laos's far north, centred on Huay Xai — the main Mekong border crossing into Thailand — and the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone, with a tourism- and border-trade-facing economy, river traffic, casino-town security, and rural ethnic-minority communities whose conservatism shapes everyday attitudes toward gender nonconformity. In the tourist and border zones, everyday scrutiny of foreign visitors is looser than in the capital, which can reduce routine attention to a trans traveller; the same zones run on checkpoint controls, casino-town security and more opaque, discretionary policing than much of the country. An outed or visibly trans visitor here is more likely to meet curiosity and gossip, refusal of lodging or services, intrusive document questions, demands for on-the-spot fines or bribes, and eviction than any formal procedure; detention risk rises mainly where an incident is linked to visa or nuisance allegations. Recourse is thin: the province has no LGBTI advocacy group or specialist support service, and border-area handling of complaints can be informal. No local pattern of trans-specific arrest, custody or violence, and no local facility rules, have been documented here — but that reflects limited documentation rather than evidence of safety, so official encounters in the border and special-economic-zone areas should be treated as unpredictable.

regions.name: Aakkâr
regions.merged_summary: Aakkâr is covered in full by Lebanon's national law on gender and sexuality, with no local exception. Lebanon's northernmost governorate is also among its poorest and most rural: an agricultural, low-service border area with Syria where security checks are routine and refugee camps including Nahr al-Bared and Beddawi sit in the countryside. It is Sunni-majority with strong clan and family authority, and conformity is enforced as much by kinship and neighbourhood networks as by officials — a visibly trans visitor is an unusual sight, and any outing can travel fast through those networks. State policing is weak and uneven, and local discretion is likely to follow conservative social mores rather than the more contested climate of the capital. Practical support is essentially absent: Lebanon's LGBT advocacy and legal-aid organisations, and the legal campaigns that have softened the national picture, are all Beirut-based, with nothing comparable operating in Aakkâr, so recourse after police hostility, family pressure or extortion is distant. Enforcement here is therefore likely less scrutinised than the national average, with no local safeguard against detention or community sanction. Incidents recorded specifically in Aakkâr are sparse; that reflects weak documentation rather than safety, and no local pattern of tolerance or mitigation offsets the national regime.

regions.name: Baalbek-Hermel
regions.merged_summary: Baalbek-Hermel is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exception. The region is a largely rural, Shia-majority part of the Bekaa Valley with strong tribal and honour norms, where Hezbollah and Amal influence shapes everyday social life and security matters; the party has publicly opposed LGBT visibility, and informal or party-linked actors can exercise moral authority alongside an uneven state presence. Unlike Beirut, the governorate has no LGBT venues, organisations, legal clinics or tourist-facing tolerance to lean on, and the capital's reformist court practice, activist networks and anonymity are effectively unavailable to a visitor here. A visibly gender-nonconforming stranger is conspicuous, and discovery is likely to reach family or clan actors as well as police, with little expectation of impartial recourse: formal legal support, NGO assistance and consular or police protection are all scarce locally, and security forces have enforced assembly restrictions in the area. A 2023 crackdown on LGBT cultural events indicates that state and party hostility is active in this zone. Public discretion may reduce day-to-day visibility but does not lower consequences once exposure occurs, and family, tribal or moral policing can escalate to detention, extortion, expulsion or violence. No trans-specific enforcement cases documented within the governorate were found, and no local protective measures or visitor-facing remedies are recorded — the absence of such records does not indicate safety, and local enforcement intensity remains uncertain.

regions.name: Beyrouth
regions.merged_summary:
Beyrouth is subject to Lebanon's national legal regime in full, with no local exception.

As the country's main tourist and commercial hub, Beirut concentrates most of Lebanon's LGBTQ venues, community organisations and legal-aid groups, and its university and nightlife districts offer more anonymity than rural areas. Central districts tend toward a more cosmopolitan, socially familiar attitude toward gender diversity than elsewhere in the country, which can reduce everyday social friction for a trans visitor. That tolerance is uneven and district-dependent, however: it varies with the officer, landlord, club or hostile group who identifies you, and it does not soften custody, prosecution or police exposure once discovery occurs. The city's visibility cuts both ways — national crackdowns concentrate where the scene exists, and documented enforcement incidents, including raids and the 2012 cinema arrest operation, took place in the city itself. Encounters with security forces at checkpoints, in nightlife raids or during public moral panics can bring detention, intrusive identity checks, extortion and mistreatment. Court rulings have limited some prosecutions but have not established reliable protection for visitors. Travelling families with a child face added scrutiny through guardianship, schools and neighbourhood reaction, and the state's economic and institutional collapse leaves avenues of recourse thin.

regions.name: Béqaa
regions.merged_summary: Béqaa is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exception. The governorate itself is largely rural and socially conservative, taking in Baalbek-Hermel, Zahle and Rashaya, with strong clan and family networks and heavy influence from Hezbollah and Amal, alongside other armed and religious actors. Informal and non-state checkpoints are common, and state authority is weaker in outlying districts than in the capital. Compared with Beirut, trans community organisations, legal clinics and secular advocacy are far thinner: the main LGBT support and legal-aid groups are Beirut-based, and documentation of incidents in the valley is sparse, so an absence of reported cases should not be read as safety. For a trans visitor who is outed, that means less anonymity in small towns, fewer places to turn, and police complaint handling that is poorer and less accountable than in Beirut — with family and community sanction, and in some areas honour-based pressure, a particular concern. Zahle's more ordinary urban commerce and hospitality economy, and Baalbek's tourism trade, offer somewhat more anonymity than the surrounding countryside, but hospitality and religious authorities there remain socially conservative. Some assessments note no documented Béqaa-specific pattern of lethal violence, while others record no local protections of any kind; no distinct regional enforcement policy against trans visitors has been established either way, and the thinness of local reporting means exposure is likely under-recorded.

regions.name: Keserwan-Jbeil
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exception. Keserwan-Jbeil is a predominantly Maronite Christian governorate immediately north of Beirut, taking in the mountain interior and the coastal towns of Jounieh and Byblos, along with Harissa. Its tourism economy — hotels and beach resorts around Jounieh, the visitor trade at Byblos — means foreign guests are routine, and staff there are accustomed to serving them. There is no Beirut-style policing of queer venues here, and no documented local criminal statute, militia policing, sanctuary practice, or separate enforcement campaign targeting trans or LGBT people; state security forces, courts and the civil registry operate under national authority, so detention and document checks follow country-wide practice, with exposure running through ordinary identity checks and hotel registration in tourist accommodation. Local reporting on incidents is thin, so the absence of a documented local pattern should not be read as tolerance. Social conditions, rather than local law, shape everyday life: the governorate is more socially conservative than the capital, where Church and family networks carry more weight, communities are smaller and village ties are tight, so anonymity is harder to keep and being outed is more likely to reach family or community. Gender nonconformity draws stronger disapproval, with conservatism enforced largely through custom and church-linked institutions rather than patrols. Alongside this, the governorate has no queer infrastructure or advocacy presence, and the legal-aid and community networks that exist in the country are concentrated in Beirut, leaving little visitor-facing safeguard or local recourse.

regions.name: Mont-Liban
regions.merged_summary:
Mont-Liban is subject to Lebanon's national law in full, with no local exemption for security forces, who operate under central Interior Ministry authority.

The governorate wraps around Beirut and its inner suburbs, mixing cosmopolitan coastal and mountain districts with strongly conservative communities. Its tourism belt — Byblos, Jounieh, Aley and the Faraya ski area — is used to foreigners and comparatively tourist-facing, and the Beirut-facing urban strip carries some of the country's highest trans and queer visibility, with nightlife and hospitality staff generally more accustomed to diversity than elsewhere in Lebanon. Everyday privacy for a foreign visitor is therefore somewhat easier to find here than in rural governorates, and community networks and legal-aid support sit close by.

Outside that strip, including conservative Christian, Druze and mixed districts, clerical and family authority is heavy and gender-nonconforming presentation can draw open hostility; social consequences for a visitor discovered tend to be harsher and recourse thinner. Hotel, landlord or stop-and-check identity scrutiny can out a traveller, inviting refusal of service, interrogation or brief detention, and enforcement of morality provisions is uneven and driven by discretion or complaints rather than local tolerance. Support organisations are concentrated in Beirut, so a visitor outside the capital's orbit may find little to fall back on. No region-specific protection exists for trans travellers: local conditions soften the day-to-day picture but do not reduce exposure if a case is taken up officially.

regions.name: Bomi
regions.merged_summary:
Bomi County is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Bomi is a small, largely rural county in western Liberia centred on its capital, Tubmanburg, with a mining and farming economy and a social life built around close-knit communities and villages where anonymity is scarce. Strong traditional and religious norms shape daily life, and a visibly transgender or gender-nonconforming visitor would be unusual and quickly noticed. The advocacy-supported private spaces that exist for LGBTQ Liberians elsewhere are concentrated in Monrovia; none are documented in Bomi, and there is no local LGBTQ or trans organisation, no hate-crime or protective machinery, and no county-level initiative offering recourse.

Institutional capacity is thinner than in the capital: the police service has limited resources and training, and there is little effective remedy or safe custody arrangement for someone whose status becomes known. Outing risk in Bomi runs through social scrutiny and everyday encounters — family, landlords, clinics, community authorities and employers — with harassment, blackmail and denunciation as realistic consequences; detention or denial of service is a more likely outcome of police contact than organised violence. No documented campaign of targeting or pattern of violence against visitors distinguishes Bomi, but the combination of low anonymity, deep conservatism, absent community infrastructure and limited institutional recourse makes outcomes harsher here than in more urban, tourist-facing parts of the country.

regions.name: Gbarpolu
regions.merged_summary:
The region is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Gbarpolu is a remote, forested and sparsely populated interior county in northwestern Liberia, centred on its capital Bopolu, with a subsistence and small-scale mining economy, limited road access and little tourism. Strong traditional and customary authority and religious conservatism shape daily life, and in small communities a visibly trans visitor is highly conspicuous: anonymity is scarce, so discovery is more likely to draw intense local curiosity, social hostility, misrecognition, service refusal or community pressure than any institutional accommodation.

Police and court presence is very thin, so practical recourse after harassment or extortion is uncertain and leans on customary and community institutions rather than state services. One local account describes basic custody placing people by birth sex. There is no trans or LGBTQ organisation or safe venue in the county, and the advocacy-run private spaces documented nationally are concentrated in Monrovia and are unlikely to be reachable from here; local health services are limited. Everyday enforcement appears less systematic than in the capital, but nothing local — no traveller-facing protection, no lighter enforcement, no documented tolerance — offsets the national regime, and local reporting is sparse, so specific incident data is limited.

regions.name: Grand Bassa
regions.merged_summary: The region is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. Grand Bassa is a rural, tightly knit coastal county centred on the port city of Buchanan, more conservative and less institutionally supported than Monrovia, with the country's LGBTQ advocacy organisations and private affirming spaces concentrated in the capital and no county-level protective measures known. In a small community where policing is uneven, discovery can bring community scrutiny, questioning, short detention or extortion, with few discreet local allies to intervene or offer rapid support. No region-specific enforcement records, documented local hostility, or local protections were found to distinguish Grand Bassa from the national picture; this absence of evidence should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Grand Cape Mount
regions.merged_summary: Grand Cape Mount is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a sparsely populated far-western coastal area around Robertsport and Lake Piso, built on fishing and subsistence farming, where police posts and courts are few and distant, church, mosque and traditional authority carry weight, and a foreign visitor stands out in small towns; there is no local LGBTQ or transgender organisation, shelter or clinic, and Monrovia's advocacy and legal-aid networks are a costly journey away. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this county from the national picture, and the absence of documented local incidents should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Lofa
regions.merged_summary:
Lofa County in northern Liberia, bordering Guinea and Sierra Leone, is a largely rural, agricultural county of small towns and border communities, with Voinjama as its principal town. The region is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions shape how that regime is experienced here. Small, tightly networked settlements with limited tourism mean a visibly transgender visitor has little anonymity, and community exposure can travel quickly through local social and family networks. Conservative Christian, Muslim and indigenous community expectations, alongside traditional authority structures, sit alongside thin policing and limited justice capacity in outlying areas, so recourse after an incident is often impractical. There is no well-established LGBTQ or trans-specific support infrastructure, anonymous private space, or advocacy presence outside Monrovia, and distance from the capital's organisations makes that support less reliable to reach. Against that backdrop, discovery of a visitor's identity carries raised risks of stigma, community exposure and extortion, and if police or courts become involved, formal protections offer thin practical cover. Organised state targeting, hostile local ordinances, or documented local incidents distinct from the national pattern are not indicated; nor is there evidence of local tolerance or protection that would distinguish Lofa favourably. Low visitor traffic may reduce how often outing occurs, but this is a matter of exposure frequency rather than of any added safeguard.

regions.name: Maryland
regions.merged_summary: Maryland County is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception or separate statute addressing gender identity or same-sex conduct. Set in remote southeastern Liberia around the coastal town of Harper, near the Ivorian border, the county is rural and tightly knit, shaped by conservative religious and customary norms. Tourism and visitor infrastructure are limited, formal policing and legal services are sparse, and local and traditional authorities carry much of the day-to-day dispute-resolving role. Health, legal-aid and transport options are thin, and the advocacy-linked private spaces that exist in the capital do not operate here, so a trans visitor would find little discreet refuge or community support. Distance from Monrovia also weakens continuity of care, official help, and practical recourse; proximity to the border adds no separate protective regime. In this setting, being outed is more likely to bring community exposure, hostile attention, humiliation, extortion, brief police custody, or denial of respectful emergency care than reliable protection, and police response to harassment or extortion of an outed foreigner is less predictable than in the capital. Travelers accompanied by a partner or minors may face added scrutiny through family and community. The county's thin institutional presence sharpens rather than softens the national picture: no local pattern of trans-specific targeting is documented, and the sparse record of local conditions should not be read as evidence of safety.

regions.name: Montserrado
regions.merged_summary:
Montserrado is Liberia's most urbanised county and contains Monrovia — the capital, the country's only significant urban centre, the international airport, and the seat of government and police headquarters. The region is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception, and no Montserrado-specific protection or distinct local enforcement pattern has been established for trans visitors.

Local conditions cut both ways. Monrovia holds the country's densest concentration of LGBTQ community infrastructure: advocacy groups including SAIL and the Transgender Network of Liberia, private gathering spaces, and a large presence of embassies, NGOs and foreign personnel. That gives a trans visitor more informal support, community contacts, witness presence and access to consular or human-rights channels than rural counties, and urban scale plus familiarity with foreigners offers some anonymity. Against this, the county hosts the police headquarters and courts that administer the national framework; reports of police corruption and extortion are common, and any custodial placement follows birth sex. Street hostility toward visible gender nonconformity can escalate into mob confrontation, with thin realistic recourse for an outed foreigner. Community contacts are reachability, not a guaranteed remedy, and the everyday outing risk is softened only modestly by the capital's relative openness.

regions.name: River Gee
regions.merged_summary: River Gee is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception. The county is a remote, sparsely populated rural area in south-eastern Liberia centred on Fish Town, built on subsistence agriculture, with very limited police, medical and judicial capacity and no tourism infrastructure. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes River Gee from the national picture: local policing practices, document checks, facilities and any county-level protections are undocumented here, so nothing about this county should be taken to soften the regime described at country level. Undocumented is not the same as safe — the national climate remains the operative one for a trans visitor, and a small, closely-knit community with thin institutional presence offers no established local safeguard against exposure.

regions.name: Rivercess
regions.merged_summary:
Rivercess, a sparsely populated coastal county in southeastern Liberia built on logging and mining with little tourism infrastructure, is subject to Liberia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Local conditions rather than any county-level rule shape a visit here. Communities are small and tight-knit, so a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner is noticed at once, and there is far less anonymity than in the capital; church-centered social life tends to read gender nonconformity as a moral offense. The advocacy networks, private support spaces and legal aid documented elsewhere in Liberia are Monrovia-based and effectively absent here, leaving no local community fallback if a visitor is outed, and the national employment non-discrimination clause has no realistic enforcement in the county. Formal state reach is thin: customary chiefly authority carries much day-to-day governance, police presence and court access are limited, and encounters with officials may be mediated by informal local expectations. Medical infrastructure is minimal, with serious cases referred to Monrovia, and no transition-related care exists anywhere in the country. County-specific police, border, detention and healthcare practices are undocumented, and no protective protocol is reported for holding a trans visitor; distance compounds any such encounter.

No county-specific incidents, protections or distinct enforcement pattern are known, and that silence should not be read as reassurance. Practical protection rests on concealment, with recourse if things go wrong distant, informal and thinly staffed.

regions.name: Anse la Raya
regions.merged_summary: Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in July 2025, and the 2022 Domestic Violence Act provides gender-neutral protection orders that expressly cover gender identity. Anse la Raya is a small, close-knit west-coast fishing village with modest local tourism and a conservative Catholic social climate. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes this quarter from the national picture on policing, legal consequences or services. In practice, the village's compact and familiar character gives a transgender visitor less anonymity than in Castries: being openly trans may draw staring, gossip, misgendering or uneven informal reactions, and local officers have less everyday experience with trans complaints than Castries-based units. The Friday fish-fry brings a flow of foreign visitors and some cover, but the village offers no trans-specific support structure.

regions.name: Canaries
regions.merged_summary: Canaries is a small, tight-knit west-coast fishing village between Soufrière and Anse La Raye, with essentially no visitor-facing trans infrastructure, little anonymity, and the nearest urban services in Castries or Soufrière. The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. No region-specific evidence was found that distinguishes Canaries from the national picture: nothing local documents distinct police practice, service refusal, local rules, or violence affecting trans visitors, and equally nothing confirms that national protections are delivered on the ground here. The village's size and setting alone establish neither hostility nor reliable access to remedies.

regions.name: Choiseul
regions.merged_summary:
Choiseul is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception.

Choiseul is a comparatively rural district on Saint Lucia's southwestern and southern coast, made up of fishing villages and subsistence farming with little tourism infrastructure — far less of a visitor presence than Castries or the northern resort belt. A transgender traveller there is conspicuous: anonymity is minimal in small, close-knit communities, and everyday outing risk is low only because there is no gay-visible scene to be discovered within, while local village and church conservatism mean that being noticed is more likely than in the capital and can bring staring, intrusive questions, misgendering, gossip, reluctance to assist or refusal of service rather than arrest or custody.

Practical support is thin. Legal aid, health services, advocacy and formal remedies are concentrated in Castries, so a visitor who needs protection or care in the south faces slower and less reliable recourse, and there is no local ordinance, protective measure or documented local police hostility either way. Low violent-crime levels in the district and small-scale community ties moderate the severity of any confrontation, but no Choiseul-specific incidents of violence against trans visitors are recorded — and that absence of local evidence should not be read as safety.

regions.name: Dennery
regions.merged_summary:
Dennery is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception, and no separate local ordinance or enforcement practice concerning transgender visitors has been identified.

Dennery is a small, predominantly Creole-speaking fishing town on Saint Lucia's Atlantic east coast — rural, close-knit and socially conservative, with modest tourism infrastructure and far less visible LGBTQ presence or support network than Castries and the northern resort belt. The same small-community character that makes it a quiet place to visit removes much of the anonymity a trans or gender-nonconforming traveller would have in a larger centre: an outsider who stands out is more likely to be recognised, stared at, questioned or gossiped about, and more exposed to open service friction or informal disclosure of who they are. Traditional and religious attitudes run stronger here than in the main visitor hubs, so social exposure is the likeliest difficulty rather than official action. Policing and complaint-handling are less centralized in this eastern quarter than in the capital, so familiarity with trans issues and the consistency of any response are thinner and less predictable if a problem does escalate. Tourism dependence means foreign guests are generally accommodated. No local incident, campaign or detention pattern involving trans visitors has been recorded in Dennery, and trans-specific treatment at local facilities and by local officers remains undocumented — that gap reflects missing information, not an assurance of safety.

regions.name: Gros Islet
regions.merged_summary: Gros Islet, Saint Lucia's northern district around Rodney Bay and Cap Estate, is the island's most tourism-oriented corridor, with a dense concentration of hotels, marinas, bars and nightlife and a visibly international visitor mix. The region is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. Within the resort zone, trans visitors are generally read as guests rather than targets: venues and staff are accustomed to serving foreign visitors, and the area's proximity to Castries, clinics, police and other services makes ordinary access to help more predictable than in remote parts of the island. The corridor is also described as more relaxed and cosmopolitan than the rural interior. Discretion still varies. Outside the tourist strip local norms are more conservative, and an outed visitor may face staring, misgendering, refusal of service or informal scrutiny; how police and health providers actually respond once a trans person is identified is not documented locally. The weekly Friday-night Gros Islet street party, known as the Jump-Up, draws large crowds and is reported as a setting where dancehall-influenced hostility toward sexual minorities can surface as verbal harassment or ejection. No trans-specific violence statistics, police practice records or enforcement patterns particular to Gros Islet were found, so the local picture rests on the district's tourism character and general community conditions rather than on documented incidents.

regions.name: Laborie
regions.merged_summary: Laborie is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. No local rule, enforcement pattern or documented case of trans-targeted policing or violence distinguishes the town from the national picture; what is distinctive is social rather than legal. Laborie is a small, quiet fishing and farming community on Saint Lucia's southwestern coast, close to Hewanorra airport and Vieux Fort but well away from the resort corridors and the LGBT infrastructure of Castries and Gros Islet. It is a traditional Creole and Catholic place where everyone is known and gossip travels fast: a visibly transgender foreign visitor should expect little anonymity, and discovery through documents or conversation is likelier here than in the capital. Social curiosity, misgendering and possible awkwardness in local shops, transport or services are the realistic frictions, rather than state or organised hostility; local violent crime is low and there is no documented pattern of residents being targeted. At the same time, the sensitisation machinery for officials is concentrated in the capital, and medical and transport infrastructure in the town itself is limited, so practical support and institutional backing are thinner than in Castries. Any incident would draw community attention quickly, and a visitor who is outed may find recourse awkward to obtain locally despite the protections available under national law. The absence of local reports of harm should be read as absence of evidence rather than assurance; discretion remains the sensible approach in a small town where visibility is high.

regions.name: Micoud
regions.merged_summary: Micoud is subject to Saint Lucia's national law in full, with no local exception. The town is a small, largely rural fishing community on the east coast with limited tourist infrastructure and few foreign visitors. No region-specific information was found distinguishing Micoud or its surrounding quarter from the national picture — there is no documented record of local police conduct, facilities practice, or incidents involving transgender visitors. That absence of documentation should not be read as confirmation of safety, and everyday encounters in lodging, services and medical care rest largely with the discretion of individual staff in a close-knit community.

regions.name: Vieux Fort
regions.merged_summary:
Vieux Fort is subject to Saint Lucia's national legal framework in full, with no local exception. The town lies on the island's southern coast and contains Hewanorra International Airport, Saint Lucia's principal international gateway, so immigration and document checks are encountered here before anywhere else; no Vieux Fort-specific practice of singling out transgender travellers or refusing foreign documents is on record, and police and border handling follows national rather than locally tailored procedures.

Vieux Fort is a smaller, close-knit southern community, generally more socially conservative and less cosmopolitan than Castries or the Gros Islet corridor, with strong church influence and no local trans-specific services, events or advocacy presence — such infrastructure is concentrated in the capital. Everyday exposure is shaped by that scale: a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor has limited anonymity, and stares, gossip, misgendering, service friction, hostile questioning or verbal hostility in streets, clubs and informal settings are plausible, with individual attitudes and discretion mattering more than formal rules.

Countering this, the town's tourism economy — beach resorts, dive operators and visitor nightlife, plus hospitality staff accustomed to international guests — tends to soften everyday friction and makes gender-nonconforming foreign travellers less anomalous than in deeply rural parishes. No pattern of anti-trans violence or official hostility toward visitors is documented locally, but that silence is not evidence of safety: no trans-specific violence data exists for Vieux Fort, and gaps around facility access, custody placement or detailed border treatment remain unresolved.

regions.name: Balzers
regions.merged_summary:
Balzers is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception, and no municipal ordinance on either side — restricting or protecting gender-nonconforming visitors — is on record.

Balzers is Liechtenstein's southernmost municipality: a small, predominantly Catholic alpine community of a few thousand residents near the Swiss border, known for Gutenberg Castle and vineyards, with a quiet, tourism-facing character and close practical ties to Switzerland. Its rule-of-law institutions are functional, and there is no documented Balzers-specific policing, exclusion, or violence directed at trans people.

The local difference is visibility rather than enforcement. In a community of this size a visibly trans visitor attracts curiosity and, at most, conservative disapproval rather than state or organised threat: staring, misgendering, or awkward interactions at a hotel or clinic are the likelier forms of friction, and discreet recourse through modest local institutions may be limited. Everyday awkwardness may be somewhat likelier here than in larger centres such as Vaduz or Schaan, but no documented pattern of targeting or service denial reaching visitors exists. Small-town visibility may also mean more casual curiosity than a traveller expects in a rural setting.

regions.name: Gamprin
regions.merged_summary: Gamprin is subject to Liechtenstein's national law in full, with no local exception. It is a small, low-lying Rhine-valley commune in the Oberland with no municipal police force of its own and no services aimed at trans visitors — policing, border control and document practice are national. A visibly trans visitor in a close-knit rural village may stand out and meet everyday curiosity or awkwardness rather than any organised local hostility, and no documented pattern of targeting or official mistreatment specific to Gamprin is known. No local ordinance, enforcement practice or reported incident was found that distinguishes Gamprin from the national picture; the absence of such reports reflects thin local documentation rather than confirmed safety.

regions.name: Mauren
